## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_How long can a robot act on a remembered scene after it loses sight of it?_

A person hidden behind a storage rack can keep moving while the robot's map still shows an empty aisle. Forgetting the person loses a constraint on motion; preserving the last position indefinitely turns old evidence into false certainty. The engineer must estimate the scene from measurements that arrive at different times with different errors, retain that estimate through brief sensing gaps, and limit how long it can support a decision. That limit depends on the motion the sensors cannot observe, the error already present, and the clearance the task can tolerate. A stored estimate must therefore carry both its physical age and the conditions under which its uncertainty remains bounded. The permission path needs that information in time to refuse motion whose evidence has expired. Spatial memory connects sensing to the causal boundary by preserving what an observation supports without extending its authority beyond the physical margin.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Apply a state estimator's predict and update steps to dated measurements, including late ones at their capture epoch, and test whether its reported covariance matches its actual error
- Track objects across frames without withholding occupancy evidence until their identity is confirmed
- Specify a spatial belief record that carries evidence age, uncertainty growth, and consumer query budgets
- Set belief expiry from bounded uncertainty growth and the task's physical tolerance
- Select a spatial representation for a clearance query from the query it answers, the memory reads it costs, and the storage it needs
- Compose transform chains at a common epoch, and trace how localization drift and loop closure move remembered map cells without renewing their evidence
- Design spatial updates that preserve evidence age and distinguish missing observations from verified free space
- Diagnose frozen transforms, phantom tracks, and unobservable drift that pass freshness and innovation checks

:::

## Spatial Belief Persistence and Expiry {#sec-memory-preserving-belief}

Every physical AI system acts on a world it observes only intermittently. Perception delivers dated, calibrated observations (@sec-perception-handoff), yet frames arrive tens of milliseconds apart, a rack upright or a gripper finger can hide the relevant surface for far longer, and the controller must keep deciding in the intervals. **Spatial memory**\index{Spatial memory} is the layer that carries physical state across those gaps. In a conventional computer, a stored value remains correct because nothing outside the machine changes what it describes. In a physical machine the stored value remains exact while the world it describes keeps moving, so a remembered state loses its truth without losing a bit. The central question of spatial memory is therefore how long a stored state may continue to authorize motion. The answer is a physical deadline rather than a software timeout, set by the error present at capture, the rate at which unobserved motion can enlarge that error, and the clearance the task can tolerate. Computing and enforcing that deadline requires five things, each developed in turn: an estimator that fuses dated measurements into a state whose reported uncertainty can be tested, a record that carries every value with its evidence epoch and an explicit error-growth law, transforms and maps that preserve those epochs through composition and update, an expiry derived from the growth law, and an account of the errors that no sensor on the machine can see.

On the warehouse mobile manipulator the question arises at every rack end. As the machine pivots away from the end of a storage rack, the rack uprights hide the cross aisle from the navigation camera, and whatever the vision backbone last detected there now survives only in memory. A person out of sight past the rack end can walk directly into the corridor that memory marks empty, and republishing the cached observation with a fresh software timestamp cannot restore the lost evidence. The stopping budget built so far defends a static obstacle at the declared clearance. A hidden person who keeps approaching changes that premise, and the expiry calculation of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion shows why that encounter needs a separately qualified crossing control or an operating restriction rather than a longer memory.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Observation age and calibrated spatial covariances are generated in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

A physical AI system therefore cannot rely solely on instantaneous sensory observations or on the context a learned policy happens to retain. It requires a **belief**\index{Belief}, an estimate of physical state carried forward from historical sensory evidence, coupled explicitly to an expanding model of uncertainty.[^fn-belief-state-record]

[^fn-belief-state-record]: **Belief State**: @astrom1965optimal showed that a controller that cannot observe its state directly loses nothing by acting on the conditional distribution of that state given everything observed so far, the formulation @sec-training-privileged-distillation meets as a partially observable decision problem. That distribution is still a mathematical object with no reference frame, no evidence epoch, and no growth law, and those three are exactly what a physical consumer needs to decide whether the belief still covers a clearance during a sensor dropout. \index{State estimation!belief state}

::: {#dfn-memory-belief-state .callout-definition title="Belief state"}

***Belief state***\index{Belief state!definition} is an estimate of a physical quantity carried forward from dated sensor evidence, stated in a reference frame, together with the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the last measurement that constrained it and a declared law for how its error bound $E(\Delta t)$ grows while no new evidence arrives.

1.  **Significance**: A belief converts elapsed time into physical error. The permission path may use it only while $E(\Delta t)$ stays within the task's tolerance, so every belief carries a deadline, its invalidation horizon counted from $t_0$, after which the permission path must refuse any motion that depends on it.
2.  **Distinction**: A measurement is evidence about one instant. A belief may describe a later instant than any of its evidence, because an estimator can propagate it forward, and it is only as good as the growth law that bounds the error of that propagation.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a recently republished belief is current. Republishing and prediction advance the publication and estimate epochs; only a new measurement advances $t_0$.

:::

Spatial memory is the second of the four proposal-side stages of Part III, between perception and intent. It sits above the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), so a remembered state can shape a proposal but cannot certify its own freshness; the permission path checks the age of the evidence against its own monotonic clock.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_sp.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense-Plan belief edge."}
*Belief carries sensing across the gap to planning.*
:::

A learned policy's context retains information according to an attention and storage budget. A person who disappears behind a pallet rack can be evicted from that context while still constraining the robot's motion, which makes an internal attention cache an unsuitable sole record of physical state. Spatial memory instead preserves the entity, its last observation, and the uncertainty that grows while it remains hidden.

Externalizing that state also separates the consumers' work. A policy retrieves a compact **spatial attention working set** around its candidate route from the host-resident scene map. An isolated permission controller instead consumes a bounded local safety snapshot, qualified for its clearance queries and available in its own memory. That snapshot preserves the source evidence epochs, uncertainty, coverage, and validity region; copying it does not make it fresh. The full map need not fit on the permission controller, and the controller must not wait for a host query to complete before deciding whether existing motion remains admissible.

Internal memory integrity alone cannot establish physical geometric validity. To prevent a machine from acting on stale data, memory systems must treat expiry as an explicit interface event. Each belief carries a deadline, its invalidation horizon (derived in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion), at which its declared error bound reaches the task's physical margin. At that deadline the belief stops supporting motion, and the permission path refuses any proposal that still depends on it and selects a feasible fallback.

Every belief, and every deadline derived from one, begins as the output of an estimator. Perception hands memory one dated, framed, and error-qualified measurement at a time (@sec-perception-observation-contract). Turning those measurements into a state that stays current between them, with an uncertainty that means what it says, is where spatial memory begins.

## Estimating State from Dated Measurements {#sec-perception-state-estimation}

A single LiDAR return or stereo match places the rack-end upright once. The permission path needs a range that stays current between sweeps, combines the LiDAR with any other qualified sensor, and reports an uncertainty that means what it says. A recursive **state estimator**\index{State estimation!recursive estimator} supplies all three by alternating two steps: a prediction that carries the state forward through a motion model, and an update that folds in each dated measurement. The Kalman filter[^fn-kalman-filter-apollo] [@kalman1960new] is the standard form of that recursion, and the rest of this chapter is built on its two steps [@thrun2005probabilistic, ch. 3; @barshalom2001estimation]. Tracking and the delayed update later in this section apply them directly. The occlusion decay of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion is the prediction step run with no update, and the observability limits of @sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds are the states no update can reach. We work the two steps once on a scalar, the remaining distance $s$ from the base to the rack-end upright, and then state them for vectors.

[^fn-kalman-filter-apollo]: **Kalman Filter**: Stanley Schmidt's group at NASA Ames took up Kálmán's paper shortly after it appeared and, for circumlunar navigation studies, linearized the nonlinear measurement equations about the current estimate [@smith1962application], the reformulation now called the extended Kalman filter. MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory then carried the filter into Apollo's on-board navigation in a square-root form suited to a computer with a short word length [@mcgee1985discovery]. The recursion fit that computer because it keeps only the latest estimate and its covariance, never the measurement history, and the same property lets spatial memory hand a consumer one dated record instead of a log to replay. \index{Kalman filter!Apollo navigation}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-aisle-kalman
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE-DIMENSIONAL KALMAN FILTER ON THE RACK-END DISTANCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-state-estimation and the consistency checks of
# │          @sec-memory-estimator-consistency.
# │
# │ Goal:    Predict the remaining distance to the rack-end upright over one
# │          LiDAR sweep, update it with the OS1-64, fuse an illustrative stereo
# │          range, and show what an arrival-stamped stereo range does.
# │ Show:    prior 20.0 mm -> 20.6 mm after prediction; LiDAR gain 0.32,
# │          posterior 17.0 mm; stereo sigma 3.8 mm at 1.10 m, gain 0.95,
# │          posterior 3.7 mm; misdating bias 38.0 mm, about 10 posterior
# │          standard deviations; expected NIS 6.25.
# │ How:     scalar predict (P + (sigma_v dt)^2) and update (g = P / (P + R));
# │          OS1-64 sweep period and worst-case precision from the registry;
# │          the illustrative stereo rig of @sec-perception-error-clearance at
# │          AISLE.d_clear; the arrival-stamp travel of @sec-perception-handoff
# │          (t_exp/2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma at the drive limit)
# │          as the misdating bias. All three inputs are re-derived here from
# │          the registry or re-loaded with guards matching Ch8's cells.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class AisleKalman:
    """Scalar predict, update, two-sensor fusion, and a misdated update on the rack-end distance."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    sigma_prior = 20.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (posterior from the previous sweep)
    sigma_v = 0.1 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (odometry speed error, e.g. wheel slip)
    dt = (1 / RM.lidar.scan_rate).to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (one 20 Hz sweep; LidarSweep.t_sweep in @sec-perception)
    sigma_lidar = RM.lidar.range_precision_max  # category: datasheet (OS1 precision, worst case, 1 sigma)
    bias_r = RM.lidar.range_accuracy  # category: datasheet (OS1 accuracy, a bias the filter cannot represent)
    z = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (range to the upright)
    b = 0.20 * meter  # category: illustrative (stereo baseline; StereoDepthError.b in @sec-perception-error-clearance)
    f_px = 800.0  # category: illustrative (focal length, pixels; StereoDepthError.f_px)
    sigma_d_px = 0.5  # category: illustrative (disparity standard deviation, pixels; StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px)
    tau_recv = (RM.nav_camera.exposure_time / 2 + RM.nav_camera.readout_time + AISLE.t_transport + AISLE.t_dma).to(
        millisecond
    )  # category: derived (ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv in @sec-perception-handoff)
    bias_misdate = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(RM.base.max_velocity, tau_recv).to(
        ureg.millimeter
    )  # category: derived (arrival-stamp travel)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    mm2 = ureg.millimeter**2
    P0 = sigma_prior.to(ureg.millimeter) ** 2
    q = ((sigma_v * dt).to(ureg.millimeter)) ** 2
    P_pred = (P0 + q).to(mm2)
    R_lidar = sigma_lidar.to(ureg.millimeter) ** 2
    g_lidar = (P_pred / (P_pred + R_lidar)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    P_lidar = ((1 - g_lidar) * P_pred).to(mm2)
    sigma_stereo = (z**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    R_stereo = sigma_stereo**2
    S_stereo = (P_lidar + R_stereo).to(mm2)
    g_stereo = (P_lidar / S_stereo).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    P_fused = ((1 - g_stereo) * P_lidar).to(mm2)
    sigma_pred = P_pred**0.5
    sigma_lidar_post = P_lidar**0.5
    sigma_fused = P_fused**0.5
    bias_post = (g_stereo * bias_misdate).to(ureg.millimeter)
    bias_in_sigmas = (bias_post / sigma_fused).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    nis_expected = 1 + (bias_misdate.to(ureg.millimeter) ** 2 / S_stereo).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dt.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Sweep period must match the perception chapter's 50 ms: {dt}")
    check(abs(tau_recv.magnitude - 26.6) < 0.05, f"Arrival offset must match the perception chapter's 26.6 ms: {tau_recv}")
    check(abs(bias_misdate.magnitude - 39.9) < 0.05, f"Arrival-stamp travel must match the perception chapter's 39.9 mm: {bias_misdate}")
    check(abs(sigma_pred.magnitude - 20.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected predicted sigma: {sigma_pred}")
    check(abs(g_lidar - 0.32) < 0.005, f"Unexpected LiDAR gain: {g_lidar}")
    check(abs(sigma_lidar_post.magnitude - 17.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected LiDAR posterior: {sigma_lidar_post}")
    check(sigma_lidar_post < min(sigma_pred, sigma_lidar), "Posterior must be tighter than either input")
    check(abs(sigma_stereo.magnitude - 3.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected stereo sigma: {sigma_stereo}")
    check(abs(g_stereo - 0.95) < 0.005, f"Unexpected stereo gain: {g_stereo}")
    check(abs(sigma_fused.magnitude - 3.7) < 0.05, f"Unexpected fused sigma: {sigma_fused}")
    check(abs(bias_post.magnitude - 38.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected misdating bias: {bias_post}")
    check(9.5 < bias_in_sigmas < 11.0, f"Prose says the bias is about ten posterior sigmas: {bias_in_sigmas}")
    check(abs(nis_expected - 6.25) < 0.05, f"Unexpected expected NIS: {nis_expected}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    sigma_prior_str = fmt_length(sigma_prior, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_v_str = fmt(sigma_v.to(meter / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    dt_str = fmt_latency(dt, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sigma_w_str = fmt_length((sigma_v * dt).to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_pred_str = fmt_length(sigma_pred, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    sigma_lidar_str = fmt_length(sigma_lidar, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    g_lidar_str = fmt(g_lidar, precision=2)
    sigma_lidar_post_str = fmt_length(sigma_lidar_post, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    z_str = fmt_length(z.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    sigma_stereo_str = fmt_length(sigma_stereo, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    g_stereo_str = fmt(g_stereo, precision=2)
    sigma_fused_str = fmt_length(sigma_fused, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    bias_misdate_str = fmt_length(bias_misdate.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    bias_r_str = fmt_length(bias_r, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    bias_post_str = fmt_length(bias_post, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    bias_in_sigmas_str = fmt(bias_in_sigmas, precision=1)
    nis_expected_str = fmt(nis_expected, precision=2)
```

The **predict** step carries the estimate forward without new evidence. Between two LiDAR sweeps, `{python} AisleKalman.dt_str` apart, odometry says the base closed the distance by $v\,\Delta t$, so $\hat{s}^- = \hat{s} - v\,\Delta t$. Odometry is itself uncertain: an illustrative speed error of `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_v_str` m/s, such as wheel slip on a polished floor, adds `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_w_str` of standard deviation over the interval. Independent errors add in variance, $P^- = P + \sigma_w^2$, so a `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_prior_str` estimate grows to `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_pred_str`. Prediction can only widen the uncertainty.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-imu-error-growth
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IMU ERROR GROWTH WITHOUT A RANGE UPDATE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The IMU paragraph of @sec-perception-state-estimation.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show from the BMI088 datasheet why white noise and constant offsets
# │          grow differently under integration, and which one limits coasting.
# │ Show:    over 1 s: 0.014 deg from gyro noise vs 1 deg from the zero-rate
# │          offset (19.2 mm at the rack end); 0.9 mm from accelerometer noise
# │          vs 98 mm from the zero-g offset, about twice delta_loc.
# │ How:     angle = N_g sqrt(T); heading = b_g T; position from white
# │          acceleration noise = N_a sqrt(T^3 / 3); position from offset =
# │          b_a T^2 / 2. BMI088 datasheet rev 1.9 (Jan 2024), Tables 4-5,
# │          typical values, from the registry (Sensors.IMU.Bosch_BMI088).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_length, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ImuErrorGrowth:
    """Attitude and position error of the BMI088 integrated open loop."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    g0 = 1.0 * ureg.standard_gravity  # category: constant (standard gravity)
    imu = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.imu  # category: datasheet (registry: Bosch BMI088)
    n_gyro = imu.gyro_noise_density.to("deg/s/Hz**0.5").magnitude  # category: datasheet (BMI088 gyro rate-noise density)
    b_gyro = imu.gyro_zero_rate_offset.to("deg/s").magnitude  # category: datasheet (BMI088 typical zero-rate offset, offset cancellation off)
    n_acc = (imu.accel_noise_density / g0).to("Hz**-0.5").magnitude  # category: datasheet (BMI088 accel noise density X/Y, in g/sqrt(Hz))
    b_acc = (imu.accel_zero_g_offset / g0).to("dimensionless").magnitude  # category: datasheet (BMI088 typical zero-g offset, in g)
    t_coast = 1.0 * second  # category: illustrative (interval without a range update)
    z = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end distance)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (along-travel localization allowance)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    T = t_coast.to(second).magnitude
    ang_noise_deg = n_gyro * math.sqrt(T)
    ang_bias_deg = b_gyro * T
    lat_bias = (z * math.sin(math.radians(ang_bias_deg))).to(ureg.millimeter)
    pos_noise = (n_acc * g0 * math.sqrt(T**3 / 3.0) * second**2).to(ureg.millimeter)
    pos_bias = (0.5 * b_acc * g0 * t_coast**2).to(ureg.millimeter)
    bias_over_loc = (pos_bias / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(ang_noise_deg - 0.014) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected gyro-noise angle: {ang_noise_deg}")
    check(abs(lat_bias.magnitude - 19.2) < 0.05, f"Unexpected lateral error from gyro offset: {lat_bias}")
    check(abs(pos_noise.magnitude - 0.91) < 0.01, f"Unexpected position error from accel noise: {pos_noise}")
    check(abs(pos_bias.magnitude - 98.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected position error from accel offset: {pos_bias}")
    check(1.8 < bias_over_loc < 2.1, f"Prose says the offset term is about twice delta_loc: {bias_over_loc}")
    check(pos_bias > 50 * pos_noise, "Prose says offsets, not white noise, limit coasting")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gyro_str = fmt(n_gyro, precision=3)
    b_gyro_str = fmt(b_gyro, precision=0)
    n_acc_str = fmt_int(round(n_acc * 1e6))
    b_acc_str = fmt_int(round(b_acc * 1e3))
    t_coast_str = fmt(T, precision=0)
    ang_noise_str = fmt(ang_noise_deg, precision=3)
    ang_bias_str = fmt(ang_bias_deg, precision=0)
    z_str = fmt_length(z.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    lat_bias_str = fmt_length(lat_bias, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    pos_noise_str = fmt_length(pos_noise, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    pos_bias_str = fmt_length(pos_bias, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
```

The machine's IMU is the other source a prediction can draw on, and its datasheet shows why it cannot carry the estimate alone for long. The BMI088's gyroscope has a rate-noise density of `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.n_gyro_str` °/s/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ and a typical zero-rate offset of `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.b_gyro_str` °/s before calibration; its accelerometer has a noise density of `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.n_acc_str` µg/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ and a typical zero-g offset of `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.b_acc_str` mg [@bosch2024bmi088]. Integration adds errors up, and the two kinds add differently. White noise adds in variance, so the angle it produces grows only as the square root of time: over an illustrative `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.t_coast_str` s without a range update it reaches `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.ang_noise_str`°. A constant offset adds linearly, so the heading error grows in proportion to time and reaches `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.ang_bias_str`° in the same second, which moves the rack-end upright `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.lat_bias_str` sideways at `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.z_str`. The accelerometer is integrated twice to reach position, so its offset grows with the square of time, $\tfrac{1}{2} b_a T^2$: `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.pos_bias_str` after one second, about twice the `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.delta_loc_str` localization allowance, while its white noise contributes only `{python} ImuErrorGrowth.pos_noise_str`. Offsets, not noise, limit how long the IMU can coast. The estimator therefore carries the offsets as extra states, which the LiDAR updates make observable, and uses the noise densities to set $\mathbf{Q}$. Because the offsets change with temperature and from unit to unit, their values on this machine come from a stationary recording on the robot, not from the datasheet.

The **update** step folds in a measurement $z$ with variance $\sigma_z^2$. The new estimate is a blend, $(1-g)\,\hat{s}^- + g\,z$, and because the two errors are independent its variance is $(1-g)^2 P^- + g^2 \sigma_z^2$. Setting the derivative with respect to $g$ to zero gives the weight that minimizes that variance, which weighs each source by the other's variance:
$$g = \frac{P^-}{P^- + \sigma_z^2}, \qquad \hat{s} = \hat{s}^- + g\,(z - \hat{s}^-), \qquad P = (1 - g)\,P^-$$
The difference $z - \hat{s}^-$ is the **innovation**\index{Innovation!definition}, what the measurement says that the prediction did not. With the OS1-64's worst-case datasheet precision of `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_str`, the gain is `{python} AisleKalman.g_lidar_str`: the filter moves a third of the way toward the LiDAR, and the posterior standard deviation falls to `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_post_str`, smaller than either input. The datasheet's precision is specified in a different scan mode from the machine's, so this input still needs confirmation at the configured rate. Its separate `{python} AisleKalman.bias_r_str` accuracy figure is a bias, which the filter's zero-mean noise model cannot represent; calibration must remove it or the clearance inset must carry it.

**Fusing a second sensor** is a second update. The illustrative stereo rig of @sec-perception-error-clearance has $\sigma_z =$ `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_stereo_str` at the `{python} AisleKalman.z_str` rack-end distance, so the gain is `{python} AisleKalman.g_stereo_str` and the fused standard deviation is `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str`. Order does not matter for independent measurements taken at the same instant; each update consumes one measurement, and the inverse variances add.

**A misdated measurement** breaks the arithmetic silently. Suppose the stereo range carries the arrival stamp of @sec-perception-handoff, so the filter pairs it with a pose `{python} AisleKalman.bias_misdate_str` farther along the aisle than the one at capture. The range then reads long by that amount, and the update pulls the estimate `{python} AisleKalman.bias_post_str` too far from the upright while reporting the same `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str` standard deviation. The error is about `{python} AisleKalman.bias_in_sigmas_str` reported standard deviations, in the dangerous direction, and nothing in the variance reveals it, because the variance update never looks at the measurement's value. This is the claim that a wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame, made concrete: a lost frame would have left the standard deviation at `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_post_str`, wider but honest.

@Fig-08-kalman-predict-update draws the same four steps as error bars on one scale, with the misdated case beside them.

::: {#fig-08-kalman-predict-update fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Predict and update on the rack-end range**: Each bar spans one standard deviation of the range estimate. Prediction widens the bar from `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_prior_str` to `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_pred_str`; the LiDAR update (gain `{python} AisleKalman.g_lidar_str`) and the stereo update (gain `{python} AisleKalman.g_stereo_str`) each narrow it below both of their inputs, whose own spreads appear as gray bars. The misdated stereo update on the right reports the same `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str` spread while sitting `{python} AisleKalman.bias_post_str` from the true range, which the variance alone cannot reveal." fig-alt="Error-bar chart with five columns on a vertical axis of range error in millimeters. Prior, predicted, after LiDAR update, and after stereo update columns are centered on zero, with the bar shrinking sharply after the stereo update. Gray bars beside the two update columns show the LiDAR and stereo measurement spreads. A fifth red column, labeled misdated stereo, has a short bar centered well above zero."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-08-kalman-predict-update
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SCALAR KALMAN PREDICT AND UPDATE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-kalman-predict-update in @sec-perception-state-estimation.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show prediction widening and each update narrowing the estimate,
# │          and a misdated update that stays narrow while biased.
# │ Show:    sigma 20.0 -> 20.6 -> 17.0 -> 3.7 mm; LiDAR and stereo input
# │          spreads; the 38.0 mm misdating bias at the fused spread.
# │ How:     Every value reads AisleKalman (no literals).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz

AK = AisleKalman
_mm = lambda q: q.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude
PETROL = "#007A87"  # measured (theme-colors.tex)
CRIMSON = "#A51C30"  # consequence (theme-colors.tex)
INK, SOFT, PALE = "#1A202C", "#4A5568", "#A0AEC0"

steps = [
    ("prior", 0.0, _mm(AK.sigma_prior), AK.sigma_prior_str, None),
    ("predict", 0.0, _mm(AK.sigma_pred), AK.sigma_pred_str, None),
    ("LiDAR\nupdate", 0.0, _mm(AK.sigma_lidar_post), AK.sigma_lidar_post_str, (_mm(AK.sigma_lidar), AK.sigma_lidar_str, AK.g_lidar_str)),
    ("stereo\nupdate", 0.0, _mm(AK.sigma_fused), AK.sigma_fused_str, (_mm(AK.sigma_stereo), AK.sigma_stereo_str, AK.g_stereo_str)),
]

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(5.4, 2.9))
ax.grid(False)
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
ax.axhline(0, color=PALE, lw=0.8, ls="--", zorder=0)

for i, (name, mu, sig, lab, meas) in enumerate(steps):
    ax.errorbar(i, mu, yerr=sig, fmt="o", color=PETROL, ms=3.5, capsize=4, lw=1.6, zorder=3)
    # sigma labels centred over their own bar so none runs into the next column's input bar
    ax.text(i, mu + sig + 1.2, f"σ = {lab}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=INK)
    if meas is not None:
        s_m, s_lab, g_lab = meas
        ax.errorbar(i - 0.42, 0.0, yerr=s_m, fmt="none", color=PALE, capsize=3, lw=1.2, zorder=2)
        ax.text(i - 0.42, -s_m - 1.2, f"input {s_lab}", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.5, color=SOFT)
        ax.text(i + 0.1, -sig - 1.2, f"gain {g_lab}", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7, color=SOFT)

# Misdated stereo update: same reported spread, biased mean
xm = len(steps) + 0.2
b = _mm(AK.bias_post)
ax.errorbar(xm, b, yerr=_mm(AK.sigma_fused), fmt="s", color=CRIMSON, ms=3.5, capsize=4, lw=1.6, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("", xy=(xm + 0.3, b), xytext=(xm + 0.3, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=CRIMSON, lw=0.8))
ax.text(xm + 0.38, b / 2, f"bias\n{AK.bias_post_str}\n≈ {AK.bias_in_sigmas_str} σ", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=7, color=CRIMSON)
ax.text(xm, b + _mm(AK.sigma_fused) + 1.2, f"σ = {AK.sigma_fused_str}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=INK)
ax.axvline(len(steps) - 0.4, color=PALE, lw=0.6)

ax.set_xticks(list(range(len(steps))) + [xm])
ax.set_xticklabels([s[0] for s in steps] + ["misdated\nstereo"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.7, xm + 1.1)
ax.set_ylabel("estimate minus true range (mm)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(-_mm(AK.sigma_lidar) - 8, max(b + 12, _mm(AK.sigma_lidar) + 6))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

For a state vector $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ with covariance $\mathbf{P}$, the same two steps use a transition matrix $\mathbf{F}$, process noise covariance $\mathbf{Q}$, a measurement matrix $\mathbf{H}$ that maps state to measurement, and a measurement covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z$ (@eq-percep-kf-predict and @eq-percep-kf-update):
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}, \qquad \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1}\mathbf{F}^\top + \mathbf{Q}$$ {#eq-percep-kf-predict}
$$\boldsymbol{\nu}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}, \quad \mathbf{S}_k = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z, \quad \mathbf{G}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{G}_k\boldsymbol{\nu}_k, \quad \mathbf{P}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{G}_k\mathbf{H})\,\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}$$ {#eq-percep-kf-update}
Here $\boldsymbol{\nu}_k$ is the innovation, $\mathbf{S}_k$ its covariance, and $\mathbf{G}_k$ the Kalman gain (written $\mathbf{G}$ so that $\mathbf{K}$ remains the camera's intrinsic matrix). The scalar example is the case $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{H} = 1$. When motion and measurement are linear and the noise is Gaussian, this update gives the minimum-variance estimate; outside those assumptions it is only a weighted correction whose covariance must be checked against data. @Sec-appendix-control-covariance develops the continuous-time counterpart.

The machine's sensors are not linear in its state. A LiDAR range to the upright is $r = \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{upright}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{base}}\|$, and a camera measures a bearing through the pinhole projection of @eq-percep-pinhole-projection. The **extended Kalman filter (EKF)**\index{Extended Kalman filter!definition} [@smith1962application] keeps @eq-percep-kf-update but replaces $\mathbf{H}$ with the Jacobian of the measurement function $h(\mathbf{x})$ evaluated at the prediction, and the predicted measurement with $h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1})$. For the range, that Jacobian with respect to the base position is the unit vector pointing from the upright toward the base. The linearization is a first-order approximation. When $h$ curves appreciably across the prior's spread, as a bearing does for a nearby object or when the prior is wide, the EKF can report a covariance smaller than its actual error [@julier2004unscented], which is one reason the consistency tests of @sec-memory-estimator-consistency are required rather than optional.

The **unscented Kalman filter (UKF)**\index{Unscented Kalman filter!definition} of @julier1997new avoids the Jacobian. It chooses $2n+1$ sigma points for an $n$-dimensional state, spread according to a square root of $\mathbf{P}$, passes each through the nonlinear function, and recomputes the mean and covariance from the transformed points [@julier2004unscented]. It captures the effect of curvature on the mean that the EKF drops, at the cost of $2n+1$ function evaluations per step, but it still summarizes the state by a mean and covariance and still needs the same qualification.

Both filters, and the tracking and delayed-update procedures built on them, assume that every measurement carries its capture epoch. The misdated example shows what happens otherwise. Its reported variance did not change while its error grew to about ten reported standard deviations, so the covariance an estimator reports is a claim that has to be tested against data.

### Testing whether the covariance is honest {#sec-memory-estimator-consistency}

Two statistics test that claim, one offline against ground truth and one at runtime against the measurements themselves. Both use the same fact: an error scaled by the covariance that is supposed to describe it has a known distribution when the covariance is honest.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-estimator-consistency
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NEES AND NIS CONSISTENCY NUMBERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-estimator-consistency (moved from the perception
# │          chapter's error-qualification cell with the estimator).
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the acceptance band for mean NEES over a finite campaign and
# │          the single-update NIS gates that one misdated update must exceed.
# │ Show:    mean-NEES band 0.65 to 1.43 (N = 50, scalar, 95 percent); NIS
# │          gates 3.84 and 6.63, which one misdated update exceeds with
# │          probability 0.63 and 0.39.
# │ How:     chi-squared quantiles (scipy.stats.chi2); noncentral chi-squared
# │          survival (scipy.stats.ncx2) for the misdated update's NIS.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from scipy.stats import chi2, ncx2
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

class EstimatorConsistency:
    """Acceptance bands and single-update gates for testing an estimator's covariance."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_runs = 50  # category: chosen (qualification runs with ground truth)
    n_dim = 1  # category: derived (scalar rack-end distance)
    conf = 0.95  # category: chosen (two-sided acceptance level)
    nis_expected = AisleKalman.nis_expected  # category: derived (misdated stereo update)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dof = n_runs * n_dim
    nees_lo = chi2.ppf((1 - conf) / 2, dof) / n_runs
    nees_hi = chi2.ppf(1 - (1 - conf) / 2, dof) / n_runs
    nis_95 = chi2.ppf(0.95, n_dim)
    nis_99 = chi2.ppf(0.99, n_dim)
    p_catch_95 = ncx2.sf(nis_95, n_dim, nis_expected - n_dim)
    p_catch_99 = ncx2.sf(nis_99, n_dim, nis_expected - n_dim)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(nees_lo - 0.65) < 0.005 and abs(nees_hi - 1.43) < 0.005, f"Unexpected NEES band: {nees_lo}, {nees_hi}")
    check(abs(nis_95 - 3.84) < 0.005 and abs(nis_99 - 6.63) < 0.005, f"Unexpected NIS gates: {nis_95}, {nis_99}")
    check(0.55 < p_catch_95 < 0.7 and 0.35 < p_catch_99 < 0.5, f"Unexpected single-update detection probabilities: {p_catch_95}, {p_catch_99}")
    check(nis_expected > nees_hi, "Prose says the averaged NIS falls far outside the band")
    # margin_misdated_update_gate_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 3.84, 6.63, 0.63, and 0.39
    check(round(nis_95, 2) == 3.84 and round(nis_99, 2) == 6.63, "Margin fig-alt gate labels are stale.")
    check(round(p_catch_95, 2) == 0.63 and round(p_catch_99, 2) == 0.39, "Margin fig-alt detection probabilities are stale.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_runs_str = fmt_int(n_runs)
    conf_pct_str = fmt_percent(conf, precision=0)
    nees_lo_str = fmt(nees_lo, precision=2)
    nees_hi_str = fmt(nees_hi, precision=2)
    nis_95_str = fmt(nis_95, precision=2)
    nis_99_str = fmt(nis_99, precision=2)
    nis_expected_str = fmt(nis_expected, precision=2)
    p_catch_95_str = fmt(p_catch_95, precision=2)
    p_catch_99_str = fmt(p_catch_99, precision=2)
```

A filter is consistent\index{Filter consistency} when its reported covariance matches its actual error. With ground truth, for example a surveyed rack-end upright and an external reference for the base pose, the normalized estimation error squared (NEES)\index{NEES!definition}, $\epsilon_k = (\mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k)^\top \mathbf{P}_k^{-1} (\mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k)$, follows a chi-squared distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom for an $n$-dimensional state when the filter is consistent. The reason is elementary: a consistent filter's error, scaled by its reported covariance, is a vector of $n$ independent standard normal variables, and a chi-squared variable with $n$ degrees of freedom is by definition the sum of their squares, so its mean is $n$. Averaged over $N$ independent runs, $N\bar{\epsilon}$ is chi-squared with $Nn$ degrees of freedom [@barshalom2001estimation]. For the scalar rack-end distance and `{python} EstimatorConsistency.n_runs_str` runs, the `{python} EstimatorConsistency.conf_pct_str` percent acceptance band for $\bar{\epsilon}$ is `{python} EstimatorConsistency.nees_lo_str` to `{python} EstimatorConsistency.nees_hi_str`. A mean above the band means the filter is overconfident, the failure that shrinks clearance; a mean below it means the reported covariance is wider than necessary, which costs speed.

Ground truth is not available at runtime, but the innovation is. The normalized innovation squared (NIS)\index{NIS!definition}, $\boldsymbol{\nu}_k^\top\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu}_k$, is chi-squared with $m$ degrees of freedom for an $m$-dimensional measurement when the models hold, and it is the same quantity the tracking gate of @eq-percep-mahalanobis-gate computes later in this section. The misdated stereo update of @fig-08-kalman-predict-update has an expected NIS of `{python} EstimatorConsistency.nis_expected_str`. Because the innovation also carries the measurement's random error, a single misdated update exceeds the 95 percent gate of `{python} EstimatorConsistency.nis_95_str` only with probability `{python} EstimatorConsistency.p_catch_95_str`, and the 99 percent gate of `{python} EstimatorConsistency.nis_99_str` with probability `{python} EstimatorConsistency.p_catch_99_str`, so a per-update gate lets a large share of such updates through. Averaged over a window of updates, the mean NIS sits several times above the consistency band, so a runtime monitor on windowed NIS detects a systematic dating error that per-update gating does not.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_misdated_update_gate_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars against a dashed slate line at the right labeled always caught. The bar for gate 3.84 reaches 0.63 of the way; the bar for gate 6.63 reaches 0.39."}

*A per-update gate catches one misdated update only `{python} EstimatorConsistency.p_catch_95_str` or `{python} EstimatorConsistency.p_catch_99_str` of the time.*
:::

### Multi-object tracking and temporal data association {#sec-perception-tracking-association}

A fresh occupied-region claim can constrain motion before the system knows which object produced it. Persistent identity serves another purpose: joining detections across frames lets the planner estimate velocity and anticipate a crossing. Detection flicker makes that association uncertain, but withholding occupancy until identity is confirmed would create an avoidable interval of blindness.

The interface therefore separates immediate geometric evidence from a **tracking-by-detection** hypothesis. The tracker associates detections, estimates motion, and carries uncertainty; persistence and expiry through missing observations are the subject of the rest of this chapter. The following state equations describe the additional information a confirmed track can supply, not a prerequisite for acting on an obstacle return.

Each active track $i$ runs the same filter on a kinematic state vector $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t = [\hat{\mathbf{p}}_t^\top, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t^\top]^\top$ with error covariance $\mathbf{P}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6\times6}$. A constant-velocity transition matrix $\mathbf{F}$ and process noise covariance $\mathbf{Q}$ propagate it between frames by @eq-percep-kf-predict.
When a new frame delivers $M$ candidate detections $\{\mathbf{z}_{t, j}\}_{j=1}^M$, the tracker must resolve **data association**,[^fn-data-association-clutter] deciding which detection belongs to which track. To prevent associating spurious sensor noise or distant objects, the tracker computes the squared Mahalanobis distance $d_{M, ij}^2$ between detection $\mathbf{z}_{t, j}$ and the predicted measurement $\mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1}$:
$$d_{M, ij}^2 = (\mathbf{z}_{t, j} - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1})^\top \mathbf{S}_{ij}^{-1} (\mathbf{z}_{t, j} - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1})$$ {#eq-percep-mahalanobis-gate}
where $\mathbf{S}_{ij} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{H}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z,j}$ is the innovation covariance of @eq-percep-kf-update and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z,j}$ is the measurement error covariance; the gated quantity is the NIS of @sec-memory-estimator-consistency. A **validation gate** evaluates @eq-percep-mahalanobis-gate and rejects any pairing where $d_{M, ij}^2 > \gamma_{\text{gate}}$, where a chi-squared threshold $\chi_3^2(1 - \alpha)$, with three degrees of freedom because the detection measures a three-dimensional position, has its nominal interpretation only under the assumed residual model. Empirical association errors require separate validation. For all gated pairs, the tracker constructs an assignment cost matrix with entries $c_{ij} = d_{M, ij}^2$ and solves the optimal global bipartite matching via the Hungarian algorithm [@kuhn1955hungarian], as the SORT tracker does [@bewley2016simple], or the Jonker-Volgenant shortest-augmenting-path algorithm [@jonker1987shortest], enforcing one-to-one assignment among the candidate pairings; it does not prove that the association is physically correct.

[^fn-data-association-clutter]: **Data Association in Clutter**: Radar tracking met this problem first. @barshalom1975tracking showed that a filter which commits to the single nearest return inside its gate can follow clutter and lose the target, and they weighted every gated return by its probability of having come from the target instead. A tracker that commits to one assignment per frame, as this one does, reveals a wrong pairing only through inconsistent innovations, which is why a confirmed track's covariance must still pass the tests of @sec-memory-estimator-consistency. \index{Data association!probabilistic}

One common track lifecycle distinguishes three states:

1. **Tentative state**: Unassociated detections spawn tentative tracks. Because false detections arise frequently from specular reflections, dust, or lens flare, the identity remains tentative until an $M$-of-$N$ confirmation rule is met. Fresh occupied-region evidence remains visible to clearance consumers during confirmation. If a downstream decision requires confirmed identity or velocity, its detection delay must include that confirmation interval; the single-frame latency waterfall of @sec-perception-latency-waterfall cannot stand in for it.
2. **Confirmed state**: Once confirmed, the track publishes its full state estimate $(\text{ID}_i, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ to the planning and intent layers. Each associated detection updates the track through @eq-percep-kf-update, which refines the mean and contracts the covariance; the correction is minimum-variance only under linear-Gaussian assumptions, so the track's covariance must pass the consistency checks of @sec-memory-estimator-consistency.
3. **Coasting state (occlusion)**: When an obstacle passes behind a warehouse shelf or is occluded by another actor, detection fails. Rather than terminating the track immediately, the system transitions the track to a coasting state. During coasting, state is propagated strictly via the motion model $\mathbf{F}$ in @eq-percep-kf-predict, and process noise $\mathbf{Q}$ adds uncertainty without a new measurement to constrain it. Downstream planners must treat coasting obstacles with expanding clearance margins. If no matching detection arrives within a timeout horizon $T_{\text{lost}}$, the identity track terminates. Termination does not establish that its last occupied region is free; the map must retain the appropriate unknown-space constraint (@sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers), and how fast a coasting track's uncertainty may grow before it stops supporting motion is the expiry question of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.

When a decision requires tracked motion, the tracker also emits an auditable **dynamic track manifest** $[(\text{ID}_k, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_k, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k, \mathbf{P}_k, t_{\text{last}}, \text{state})]$. Downstream intent filters in @sec-intent-admissible-goal-sets consume these velocities and covariances to establish dynamic exclusion cones, while safety enforcers in @sec-enforcement evaluate stopping clearance against moving targets.

### Applying a delayed observation {#sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation}

Tracking assumes that each detection arrives in capture order. A camera frame that spends tens of milliseconds in inference can arrive after a faster sensor's later measurement has already updated the state. The capture epoch the observation contract preserves (@sec-perception-observation-contract) makes such a delayed measurement usable when the estimator has a qualified history and motion model. The notation is that of @eq-percep-kf-update: $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ the estimated state, $\mathbf{P}$ its covariance, $\mathbf{H}$ the measurement model, and $\mathbf{G}$ the Kalman gain. @Sec-appendix-control-lqr develops the estimation/control relationship.

A delayed visual observation must correct the state at its capture epoch before the estimator propagates the correction to the present. One implementation retains historical states and inertial inputs in an **out-of-sequence ring buffer** with $N_{\text{buffer}} = \lceil T_{\text{buffer}} / \Delta t_{\text{IMU}} \rceil$ slots. Its horizon $T_{\text{buffer}}$ bounds the delay it can accommodate. When observation $\mathbf{z}_{t_0}$ arrives at $t_{\text{recv}}$, the estimator retrieves the prediction at $t_0$, computes its innovation and gain, and applies the update of @eq-percep-kf-update at that epoch (@eq-percep-oosm-correction):
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0-1} + \mathbf{G}_{t_0} (\mathbf{z}_{t_0} - \mathbf{H}_{t_0} \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0-1}), \quad \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{G}_{t_0}\mathbf{H}_{t_0}) \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0-1}$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-correction}
For the following propagation-only replay, assume no intervening measurement updates. If other sensors corrected the state during the interval, their updates must also be replayed in timestamp order. The estimator then executes a fast replay pass, re-integrating buffered IMU samples from $t_0$ to $t_{\text{recv}}$ using the updated initial condition $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0}$, to bring the current state estimate $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{recv}}}$ into alignment with the new observation without introducing non-causal state discontinuities (@eq-percep-oosm-replay):
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{recv}}} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0} + \sum_{k = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{f}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \Delta t_{\text{IMU}}$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-replay}
with covariance forward replay governed by state transition matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) = \prod_{k = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{F}_k$:
$$\mathbf{P}_{t_{\text{recv}}} = \mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0} \mathbf{\Phi}^\top(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) + \sum_{k = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, k+1) \mathbf{Q}_k \mathbf{\Phi}^\top(t_{\text{recv}}, k+1)$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-cov-replay}
This rewind-and-replay routine (@eq-percep-oosm-cov-replay) is strictly bounded by ring buffer horizon $T_{\text{buffer}}$. If pipeline jitter or memory bus contention stretches observation age such that $t_{\text{age}} > T_{\text{buffer}}$, the ring buffer has already overwritten epoch $t_0$. The estimator must refuse the delayed measurement, allow process noise $\mathbf{Q}$ to inflate the predictive covariance $\mathbf{P}$, and alert the downstream permission path that visual grounding has lapsed.

**Observation tokens in end-to-end VLA policies**: A learned policy that consumes the delayed observation faces the same out-of-sequence problem without a ring buffer. The observation tokenizer proposed in @sec-perception-observation-contract gives it the elapsed time and propagated state that the estimator uses here; it does not validate the estimate or grant the resulting action permission.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-checkpoint-estimator
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ESTIMATOR CHECKPOINT: GUARD ON THE GAIN ESTIMATE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @chk-mem-estimator-tracking (the gain-estimate item).
# │
# │ Goal:    Guard the verdict the checkpoint's estimate item expects without
# │          printing the answer: with the stereo spread doubled, stereo still
# │          dominates the fused estimate.
# │ Show:    nothing (guards only); the item quotes AisleKalman's strings.
# │ How:     g = P / (P + (2 sigma_stereo)^2) with P the LiDAR posterior.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class EstimatorCheckpoint:
    """Guards for the estimator checkpoint's estimate item (answers stay private)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    factor = 2.0  # category: chosen (checkpoint given: stereo spread doubled)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    P = AisleKalman.P_lidar
    R = (factor * AisleKalman.sigma_stereo) ** 2
    g = (P / (P + R)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    sigma = ((1 - g) * P) ** 0.5

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.5 < g < AisleKalman.g_stereo, f"Doubled stereo spread must lower the gain yet keep stereo dominant: {g}")
    check(AisleKalman.sigma_fused < sigma < AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_post, f"Fused spread must sit between the two cases: {sigma}")
```

::: {#chk-mem-estimator-tracking .callout-checkpoint title="The estimator behind every belief"}

Every belief the rest of the chapter ages is the output of this estimator. These items test whether you can run it and whether you can tell when its reported uncertainty is honest.

- [ ] **Predict vs. update**: Can you explain why a prediction step can only widen the reported variance, while an update narrows it below both the prediction and the measurement?
- [ ] **Gain estimate**: If the stereo range's standard deviation doubled from `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_stereo_str`, with the LiDAR-updated `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_post_str` prior unchanged, what would the stereo gain and the fused standard deviation be, and which sensor would then dominate the fused estimate?
- [ ] **Estimator consistency**: Can you explain why a misdated update leaves the reported variance unchanged, and why a windowed NIS monitor catches the systematic dating error that a per-update gate lets through?
- [ ] **Occupancy vs. identity**: Can you explain why a tentative track's occupied region must reach clearance consumers before confirmation, and what a decision that needs confirmed velocity must add to its detection delay?
- [ ] **Late measurements**: Can you explain what the estimator must do with a measurement whose age exceeds its ring buffer's horizon, and why?

:::

The estimator's output is what spatial memory stores: a state, its tested covariance, the instant the state describes, and the capture epochs of the measurements that last constrained it. Prediction and delayed replay keep the state current, but only a measurement adds evidence, and neither step moves the evidence epochs forward. That output must also leave the estimator in a form a consumer can check. A belief that must declare its own expiry has to travel with more than its value, so the first handoff question is what a consumer needs to evaluate a stored value after its sensor loses sight of the object.

## The Spatial Memory Handoff and State Invariants {#sec-memory-handoff}

A position vector arriving over an inter-process bus cannot identify the entity, quantity, or units it describes. The same numbers could denote a workpiece center in meters, a joint angle in radians, or a contact force in newtons. A consumer needs those distinctions before applying a control law; a meters-to-millimeters mismatch alone changes the interpreted displacement by a thousandfold. The spatial belief record therefore begins with entity identity, physical quantity, and measurement units, rather than relying on conventions hidden in the producing model or transport wrapper.

Specifying the quantity and units remains incomplete without binding the value to a concrete reference frame. Identical spatial coordinates describe entirely different physical realities depending on the origin and orientation of the coordinate system. A Cartesian position $[0.142, -0.051, 0.812]\text{ m}$ designates a point suspended in free space when evaluated in the robot base frame\index{Base frame}, but represents a point several hundred millimeters inside a rigid fixture when interpreted in the tool flange frame\index{Tool flange frame}. Because kinematic links flex, joints move, and coordinate transforms update at varying rates, a belief record must carry an explicit frame identifier. Carrying the frame allows the receiving node to look up the corresponding spatial transformation tree and project the stored geometry into the local frame required by the actuator, preventing the controller from acting on geometric misalignments caused by moving kinematic chains.

Geometry and identity describe physical state at a single moment, but spatial memory must also capture the temporal anchor of that state. The record carries the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the physical interaction or optical exposure that last constrained the estimate at the causal boundary. In distributed machine architectures, intermediate nodes often republish data, execute Kalman filter prediction steps, or run forward kinematic propagations to maintain high-rate control streams; none of these computational steps adds physical evidence. The evidence epoch must therefore pass unchanged through every republish, filter, and prediction stage, so that consumers measure the age of the information against the physical world rather than against the scheduling frequency of the local computer.

The anchored belief is the output of the multi-sensor state estimator\index{State estimation!contract boundary}\index{Sensor fusion!informational contract} of @sec-perception-state-estimation, which combines asynchronous measurements with a motion model to infer the state between them, and whose reported covariance the tests of @sec-memory-estimator-consistency check against the actual error. Consumers need the resulting state, its justified error model, and the physical evidence that constrains each relevant component. They do not need to reproduce the estimator. A prediction step advances the estimate epoch while its evidence continues aging; a fresh measurement renews only the state dimensions it actually constrains. The covariance propagation mechanics are collected in @sec-appendix-control-covariance. Here the engineering obligation is to expose bounded growth through occlusion and withdraw claims whose assumptions no longer hold.

Knowing the evidence epoch $t_0$ establishes elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$, but elapsed time alone cannot determine whether a belief is valid for a given action. Two estimates of identical age diverge at different rates depending on physical constraints. The rack end itself is bolted to the floor, so its remembered position can remain useful while the machine's localization bound and the fixed-rack premise hold, whereas a person hidden behind it can move at walking speed and close the narrow gap beside it before the next camera frame arrives.

The minimum record fields necessary for a consumer to evaluate a stored state can be derived directly from the requirement to bound current error. Let $E(\Delta t)$ represent the upper bound of the discrepancy between the stored value and true physical state after an elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$. If an estimator establishes a state at time $t_0$ with an initial uncertainty bound\index{Uncertainty bound} $E_0$, and external disturbances or unmodeled velocities cause the true state to diverge at a maximum rate $r$, the upper bound on error at current time $t$ obeys the linear expansion\index{Error expansion} $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r\,\Delta t$. At the rack end the stored claim is spatial, that no person stands near the machine; $E_0$ is then the machine's localization error, $r$ is the walking speed at which a person the rack hides can advance on the machine, and the tolerance is the depth of observed free space the machine does not need as clearance. @Sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion evaluates that law. Under the stochastic acceleration-noise model of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion, double integration produces cubic growth of position variance ($\propto t^3$). Omitting the initial bound or the dynamic growth terms leaves the consumer unable to compute $E(\Delta t)$, so an initial bound and an explicit expansion model are both structurally required fields of the record.

Expressing uncertainty through physical bounds and expansion rates distinguishes a physical AI belief from a probabilistic confidence score. An object detection network might output a class confidence of $0.94$, but that softmax score is not calibrated evidence (@sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities), and a downstream position controller cannot convert a unitless probability into a safe actuator displacement margin (i.e., how far the arm can physically move before risking a collision). A confidence score of $0.94$ provides no information about whether an obstacle boundary is uncertain by $2.0\text{ mm}$ or by $200\text{ mm}$, nor does it indicate how rapidly that boundary moves when occlusion occurs. A physical memory record must express its initial bound $E_0$ and expansion rate $r$ in concrete physical dimensions such as meters, radians, or newtons per second. Furthermore, these rates are valid only within a declared validity region, such as a maximum assumed acceleration or a verified contact friction coefficient. If physical operating conditions leave that region, the expansion rate no longer holds, and the belief record must be treated as invalid.

When the gripper finger approaches the latch-release slot, the consumer compares the belief's current error with the slot clearance. It converts the evidence epoch into its own clock, includes the clock-conversion bound, and evaluates the declared growth law at the time the state will be used. This is a continuing obligation during execution, not a one-time path-generation check. A new proposal whose evidence fails the check is refused without automatically revoking a still-valid active command. If the active motion itself depends on expiring evidence, the controller must begin a feasible fallback early enough that the response remains within the available clearance. The belief's expiry is a limit on supported motion, not a promise that an instantaneous stop is possible at that instant.

The fields this section has derived travel together as the **spatial belief record**\index{Spatial belief record!definition}\index{Belief record!definition}, the seventh record in the record chain. It binds identified physical quantities and map regions to a reference frame, hardware evidence epochs, estimate epochs, clock-conversion bounds, uncertainty-growth laws, operating validity regions, task expiries, provenance, and lifecycle status, and it gives each consumer a query-work limit derived from that consumer's deadline rather than imposed on every scene representation. A classification score, a map publication time, or a transform value alone cannot supply that contract, because none couples physical units and evidence age to an error-growth law. The record makes the claims checkable; qualification must establish that they hold. Nor may a consumer wait for an upstream publisher to announce expiry: if that publisher's thread hangs or its messages stop, the consumer must still age the evidence and enforce its own deadline. @Tbl-09-invalidation-epochs in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema lays the record out field by field.

Evaluating the spatial belief record depends on calculating the elapsed time $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$ against physical reality. If the consumer cannot verify the exact physical instant when energy transduction occurred, the calculated error bound $E(\Delta t)$ becomes an unanchored fiction, mistaking software compute cycles for physical evidence. The estimate epoch and clock conversion named in the record exist to protect that anchor, while provenance and lifecycle status, the record's remaining fields, are developed with the schema in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.

## State Epochs and Temporal Anchoring {#sec-memory-state-epoch}

A bounding box or 3D Gaussian pose emitted by a neural object detector describes where an entity was when photons struck the camera CMOS sensor, not where it is when the inference tensor arrives in memory. Every spatial claim refers to a specific physical instant, its **epoch**\index{Epoch}, and any state crossing a physical AI pipeline carries three distinct epochs before an actuator can fire. The **acquisition epoch**\index{Epoch!acquisition} ($t_0$) is the capture epoch of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract), the observation's physical time reference, such as the exposure midpoint for the camera or the instant a hardware register latches an encoder count. Spatial memory anchors it as its evidence epoch. Spatial memory adds the two epochs that follow it. The **estimate epoch**\index{Epoch!estimate} ($t_{\text{est}}$) marks the physical instant that the estimated state describes. A predictor can advance that instant beyond the last observation without obtaining new evidence; the time at which computation finishes is a separate scheduling fact. The **publication epoch**\index{Epoch!publication} ($t_{\text{pub}}$) marks the instant the serialized state record was committed to the transport bus or shared-memory ring buffer for dispatch to downstream consumers.

Collapsing these three timestamps into one receipt or transmission timestamp destroys the physical anchor. This **publish-time stamping anti-pattern**\index{Publish-time stamping anti-pattern!definition} occurs when a wrapper stamps its output with the current software clock after exposure, transport, inference, and postprocessing have already elapsed. The receiver then sees a recent message containing old evidence. The age-as-displacement relation established in @sec-perception-photons-to-claims still applies throughout that pipeline. Publication time helps diagnose scheduling delay, but only acquisition time lets a motion consumer account for the world's change since the measurement.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The hardware capture stamp this anti-pattern discards is defined in @sec-perception-handoff.
:::

Even when a system records true acquisition epochs, physical AI architectures rely on distributed processing nodes whose local oscillator clocks drift independently. The deployed clock-conversion protocol must establish an error bound under its stated load and fault conditions; a bus interface alone supplies no such guarantee. That temporal uncertainty becomes spatial uncertainty at the relative speed of whatever the record describes.[^fn-clocksync-error-bound] The observation record of @sec-perception-observation-contract already carries this bound as its clock-conversion error, and a belief built from that observation keeps it. Every consumer adds the bound to the evidence age before judging freshness, and the error budget allocates the distance that bound covers at the record's relative speed alongside sensor resolution and structural deflection. In safety enforcement, downstream Control Barrier Functions treat this clock-synchronization uncertainty $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ as an irreducible temporal margin, inflating the required spatial barrier clearance by $d_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ before granting motor torque authorization.

[^fn-clocksync-error-bound]: **Clock Synchronization Bound**: CAN-FD bit-phase synchronization aligns bit sampling within one frame; it does not align the distributed clocks that date physical observations. PTP and EtherCAT Distributed Clocks provide synchronization mechanisms, but their names alone do not establish the deployed error bound, which only a measurement under the stated load and fault conditions supplies. \index{Fieldbus!synchronization jitter}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-epoch-alignment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE SAMPLING EPOCHS FOR FUSION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-state-epoch (three sensors latch at different epochs).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that fusing two observations requires projecting one across
# │          the gap between their acquisition epochs.
# │ Show:    tactile 12 ms, camera 18.5 ms, encoders 21 ms; camera-to-encoder
# │          gap 2.5 ms.
# │ How:     Illustrative epochs in one cycle; the gap is |t3 - t2|.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

class MemoryEpochAlignment:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t1 = 12.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (tactile array latches force)
    t2 = 18.5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (camera exposure midpoint)
    t3 = 21.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (encoders sample angles)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    gap = abs(t3 - t2).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t1 < t2 < t3, "The illustrative epochs must be in sampling order.")
    check(abs(gap.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, "Camera-to-encoder gap is 2.5 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t1_str = fmt_latency(t1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t2_str = fmt_latency(t2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t3_str = fmt_latency(t3, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gap_str = fmt_latency(gap, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Physical systems often combine asynchronously acquired signals, even though hardware triggers can align selected sensors. In an illustrative asynchronous cycle, a tactile array might latch normal force readings at $t_1 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, an optical tracking camera might have its exposure midpoint at $t_2 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and joint optical encoders might sample angular positions at $t_3 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str`. These observations occur at different epochs and cannot be combined through direct tensor concatenation or algebraic operations. In multimodal foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, visual tokens, proprioceptive vectors, and tactile embeddings are frequently packed into a single attention sequence under the implicit assumption that all tokens capture a simultaneous physical snapshot. Nothing in that packing records that the hand position came from $t_2$ and the joint reading from $t_3$, so whatever the model infers from their combination carries no bound on the error the mismatch introduces. Fusing a camera observation at $t_2$ with an encoder observation at $t_3$ requires the consumer to project one state across the temporal gap $\Delta t = |t_3 - t_2| =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` using explicit kinematic models and bounded velocities (for example, propagating the historical camera observation along the joint velocity vector to reconcile it with the instantaneous encoder reading). Without the true acquisition epoch for each individual signal, the alignment calculation cannot determine the sign or magnitude of $\Delta t$, compounding geometric errors across every inference cycle (@fig-09-epoch-alignment).

::: {#fig-09-epoch-alignment fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three evidence epochs in one cycle**: The tactile array, the camera's exposure midpoint, and the joint encoders each date their evidence on one clock, at `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str` in this illustrative cycle. A fused state dated to the encoder epoch must carry the camera's evidence across the `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` gap with a kinematic model and a bounded velocity; packing the three readings into one token sequence records none of these epochs." fig-alt="Timing strip with three lanes labeled tactile, camera, and encoders over a time axis in milliseconds. Each lane has one short sample mark at its own time, with vertical event lines labeled tactile latch, camera exposure midpoint, and encoder sample. A bracket above the strip spans the interval between the camera and encoder marks and is labeled with the gap to project across."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-memory-epoch-alignment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THREE EVIDENCE EPOCHS ON ONE CLOCK (TIMING STRIP FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-09-epoch-alignment in @sec-memory-state-epoch
# │ Goal:    show that each sensor dates its evidence at its own epoch and that
# │          fusion must project across the gap between them
# │ Show:    the tactile, camera, and encoder epochs; the camera-to-encoder gap
# │ How:     viz.TimingStrip / plot_timing_strip; every time from the
# │          MemoryEpochAlignment cell; sample marks have a nominal drawing
# │          width only
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
MEA = MemoryEpochAlignment
t1 = MEA.t1.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: illustrative (from the cell)
t2 = MEA.t2.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: illustrative (from the cell)
t3 = MEA.t3.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: illustrative (from the cell)
w = 0.25  # drawing width of a sample mark (ms); not a physical duration

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
strip = viz.TimingStrip(
    spans=[
        viz.Span("", t1 - w / 2, t1 + w / 2, "measured", 0, solid=True),
        viz.Span("", t2 - w / 2, t2 + w / 2, "measured", 1, solid=True),
        viz.Span("", t3 - w / 2, t3 + w / 2, "measured", 2, solid=True),
    ],
    lanes=["tactile", "camera", "encoders"],
    events=[
        viz.Event(t1, f"tactile latch {MEA.t1_str}", "measured", 1),
        viz.Event(t2, f"exposure midpoint {MEA.t2_str}", "measured", 0, ha="right"),
        viz.Event(t3, f"encoder sample {MEA.t3_str}", "measured", 0, ha="left"),
    ],
    brackets=[viz.Bracket(t2, t3, f"project across {MEA.gap_str}", "neutral", "time", 0)],
    xlim=(t1 - 3, t3 + 5),
    figsize=(6.2, 2.4),
    xlabel="Time in the cycle (ms)",
)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs((t3 - t2) - MEA.gap.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The bracket must span the cell's camera-to-encoder gap.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, _ = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip)
plt.show()
```

:::

With these epochs and the clock-synchronization bound carried in the record of @sec-memory-handoff, the consumer computes the elapsed duration between the evidence epoch and the execution deadline, evaluates the worst-case expansion of the error bound, and determines whether the state remains within task tolerances. Handing over a state without its acquisition epoch leaves the consumer blind to transport delays and scheduling jitter, turning deterministic control into open-loop guesswork. Because physical geometry also changes as bodies move through space, spatial transforms between reference frames are subject to the same temporal decay, carrying their own distinct evidence epochs.

## Coordinate Transform Expiry and Localization Drift {#sec-memory-reference-frames}

A coordinate frame binds a spatial representation, but in an active physical machine the frame itself moves. In embodied architectures, sensors, chassis links, and end-effectors are related through a directed acyclic transform graph. What the static graph does not show is how an edge goes stale. Each edge of the tree in @fig-09-robot-transform-tree stores a rigid-body pose parameterized by joint angles [@lynch2017modern; @craig2005introduction], and that pose describes the machine only at the epoch when its physical geometry was transduced. When an onboard computer chains transforms measured at different times, because of neural inference latency, transport delay, asynchronous sensor sampling, or dropped frames, the mathematical product is a hybrid pose that the physical machine never occupied (@sec-appendix-control-spatial defines coordinate mapping and transform-chain composition).

A transform also spans several machine words (six or seven floating-point numbers for translations and rotation quaternions), so a high-rate control reader racing an asynchronous vision writer can observe an old rotation paired with a new translation. The lock-free seqlock mailbox established in @sec-nervous-cadences closes this concurrency race without blocking hard real-time control threads: each reader makes one bounded attempt per tick and never waits; a torn read is discarded, and the last validated transform ages in its place.

::: {#fig-09-robot-transform-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator kinematic frame tree and temporal dynamics**: Articulated seven-joint manipulator geometry (a) and the corresponding coordinate transform tree in ROS \\texttt{tf2} (b), in which every frame has exactly one parent. Each tree edge stores a homogeneous transformation matrix parameterized by joint state. The target's pose hangs from the base frame, stamped with the epoch $t_0$ of the wrist-camera measurement that produced it, so composing it with the current joint chain mixes epochs, and a wrist rotation $\\Delta\\theta$ over the interval swings the tool center point by $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$ (adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013 [@craig2005introduction; @foote2013tf])." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel a: a seven-joint arm on a base labeled base_link, joints numbered 1 to 7, a gripper whose tool center point is labeled tool0, and a wrist camera mounted on the flange.
