A dimension line labeled ℓ spans from joint 7, the wrist, to the tool center point, and a red dashed line turned by Δθ about the wrist shows the tool displaced by e_tool ≈ ℓ Δθ. Panel b: a tree with world at the root, then base_link, then a link1 to link7 chain annotated with joint angles at time t, whose children are wrist_cam and tool0. A red dashed edge labeled stamped t0 connects base_link to target_object, and a dotted teal path from wrist_cam to target_object is labeled camera measurement at t0, not a tree edge. A legend distinguishes tree edges, edges dated at an older epoch, and measurements."}
![](images/svg/fig09_canonical_robot_frame_tree.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-09-robot-transform-tree, panel (a) illustrates the physical geometry of an articulated serial manipulator carrying an eye-in-hand wrist camera and an end-effector tool center point (`tool0`). Mechanical links (`link1` through `link7`) are connected by revolute joints whose optical encoders continuously sample joint angles $\theta_i(t)$. The tool tip extends beyond the wrist joint by an effective lever arm $\ell$. When the wrist turns at angular rate $\omega$, any temporal latency $\Delta t$ in the wrist coordinate frame introduces an angular lag $\Delta\theta = \omega\,\Delta t$, sweeping the tool tip across an unmodeled circular arc $e_{\text{tool}} \approx \ell\,\Delta\theta$.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-transform-tree-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TRANSFORM-TREE EDGE RATES ON THE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The transform-tree paragraph of @sec-memory-reference-frames.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that the tree's edges arrive at different rates on the
# │          running machine: arm joint state at the joint-control rate, the
# │          vision edge at the wrist camera's frame rate.
# │ Show:    arm joint-control rate; wrist-camera frame rate; their ratio.
# │ How:     Registry values; ratio = f_joint / f_camera.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class TransformTreeRates:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    f_joint = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.arm.control_frequency  # category: datasheet (Panda joint-control rate)
    f_camera = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.wrist_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (wrist camera frame rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ratio = (f_joint / f_camera).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ratio > 10, "Joint edges must arrive an order of magnitude more often than vision edges.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    f_joint_str = fmt_frequency(f_joint, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    f_camera_str = fmt_frequency(f_camera, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
```

Panel (b) depicts the corresponding coordinate transform tree maintained as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in robot middleware such as ROS `tf2` [@foote2013tf]. Each directed edge represents a $4 \times 4$ homogeneous transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}_{A \leftarrow B}$ mapping points from child frame $B$ into parent frame $A$. Because the arm's joint state arrives at its `{python} TransformTreeRates.f_joint_str` joint-control rate over the deterministic fieldbus while the wrist camera's perception pipeline publishes target poses (`target_object`) at the camera's `{python} TransformTreeRates.f_camera_str` frame rate over an asynchronous transport, the transform tree inevitably buffers edges with disparate timestamps. The library itself refuses to mix them. A `tf2` lookup for a chain at time $t$ resolves every edge at that same $t$, interpolating each edge between its buffered samples, and it raises an extrapolation error when $t$ lies beyond an edge's latest sample; a request for "the latest" transform returns the chain at the latest time common to all its edges, which is again a single consistent epoch [@foote2013tf]. Hybrid poses come from application code that bypasses those semantics. A node that caches an edge, composes an object pose carried in a detection message with a separate lookup of the arm at "now," or republishes an old edge under a new stamp multiplies the current forward kinematics $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{wrist}}(t)$ with a stale vision edge $\mathbf{T}_{\text{wrist} \leftarrow \text{object}}(t - \Delta t)$. That composition is the **chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern**\index{Chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern!definition}: an unphysical hybrid pose that the robot never occupied.

The same-time rule leaves the application one decision, what to do when the requested time lies beyond the newest sample. A lookup can fail immediately, or a noncritical caller can wait subject to a timeout. The permission path requires bounded, nonblocking lookup and explicit rejection on failure. An application that instead predicts the transform must carry a validated growth bound; naive extrapolation during a communication stall otherwise accumulates lever-arm error $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$.

The cost of an expired transform is direct spatial displacement (@fig-frame-staleness-error). Applying the age-as-displacement relation of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims to kinematics, uncompensated latency translates directly into geometric positioning error through the lever arm of the linkages. @Sec-appendix-control-spatial derives this kinematic error propagation from the cross product.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE SLOT-TO-FINGER TRANSFORM AT THE LATCH SLOT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-reference-frames (lever-arm staleness example); owns
# │          the latch-slot constants that @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion
# │          (LatchSlotBelief) reads.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one missed wrist-camera frame on the slot-to-finger
# │          edge can spend more than the latch-release slot's tolerance, most
# │          of it through the lever arm.
# │ Show:    the frame period, the lateral drift at the finger's drift bound,
# │          the lever-arm arc, and their sum with E0 against the slot.
# │ How:     e_tool ~ E0 + v_drift dt + l omega dt, dt one wrist-camera frame.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchTransformStaleness:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    frame_rate = RM.wrist_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (wrist camera)
    e0 = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (finger-to-slot error at the wrist capture)
    v_drift = 12.0 * ureg.millimeter / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (unobserved lateral velocity error bound)
    e_max = 1.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (latch-release slot tolerance)
    lever = 0.15 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (wrist-to-fingertip lever arm)
    omega = 0.30 * ureg.radian / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (wrist rate while aligning the finger)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    e_trans = (v_drift * dt).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_rot = (lever * omega * dt / ureg.radian).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_tool = (e0 + e_trans + e_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ratio = (e_tool / e_max).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dt.magnitude - 16.667) < 1e-3, f"Wrist-camera frame period should be 16.7 ms, got {dt}.")
    check(abs(e_trans.magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-6, f"Lateral drift over one frame should be 0.20 mm, got {e_trans}.")
    check(abs(e_rot.magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-6, f"Lever-arm arc should be 0.75 mm, got {e_rot}.")
    check(e_rot > e_trans, "The lever arm must contribute more than the lateral drift.")
    check(e_tool > e_max, "One missed frame must exceed the slot tolerance.")
    check(abs(e_tool.magnitude - 1.05) < 1e-6, f"Total finger error should be 1.05 mm, got {e_tool}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt_str = fmt_latency(dt, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    e0_str = fmt_length(e0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drift_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    lever_str = fmt_length(lever, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, precision=2)
    e_trans_str = fmt_length(e_trans, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_rot_str = fmt_length(e_rot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_tool_str = fmt_length(e_tool, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    ratio_pct_str = fmt_percent(ratio - 1, precision=0, style="prose")
```

How little staleness it takes to spend a task's tolerance shows at the latch-release slot, while the wrist camera can still see it. Each wrist-camera frame, one every `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.dt_str`, renews the slot's pose in the camera frame and with it the slot-to-finger edge the controller aligns on, and the finger must stay within the slot tolerance $E_{\max}$ of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_max_str`. To isolate the effect of one frame period, suppose the supporting observation is available at its capture epoch, with ingestion delay idealized as zero, and the edge then ages by one frame period. A deployed edge is already older when ingestion completes; its consumer must qualify and charge the full capture-to-use age, including processing, transport, and any additional missed frames. Starting from an initial error of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e0_str`, the finger's lateral offset drifts at most $e_{\text{trans}} = v_{\text{drift}}\,\Delta t$ under an illustrative `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift_str` bound on its unobserved lateral velocity, validated for the arm's operating region, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_trans_str`. With the fingertip an illustrative $\ell$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.lever_str` beyond the wrist and the wrist turning at an illustrative $\omega$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.omega_str` as it aligns the finger, the lever arm adds $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_rot_str`. The joint encoders measure that turn, but an application that composes the cached slot edge, dated to the previous frame, with the current wrist pose obtains a hybrid pose, a finger position the arm never held. Only chaining the slot against the wrist pose of its own capture epoch, which a same-time lookup does, or expiring the edge, removes that arc. Left in the chain, the stale edge misplaces the finger by `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str`, `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.ratio_pct_str` more than the slot allows, and more of that error comes from the lever arm than from the drift. Because the hand-composed product evaluates without error, nothing flags the stale pose, and the controller keeps aligning the finger on a slot position that is off by more than the clearance, which on an unfavorable approach puts the finger against the strike plate beside the slot.

::: {#fig-frame-staleness-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot**: Illustrative finger error over one frame period, with zero ingestion delay assumed to isolate this contribution. A deployed calculation must use full capture-to-use age. The slot-to-finger edge ages by duration $\\Delta t$. Lateral drift at the velocity bound $v_{\\text{drift}}$ moves the finger by $e_{\\text{trans}} = v_{\\text{drift}}\\,\\Delta t$, while the wrist turning at $\\omega$ swings the fingertip, a lever arm $\\ell$ beyond it, by $e_{\\text{rot}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\omega\\,\\Delta t$. Composing the stale edge with the current wrist pose adds both to the initial error $E_0$, so the finger error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx E_0 + e_{\\text{trans}} + \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$ exceeds the slot tolerance $E_{\\max}$." fig-alt="Transform staleness at the latch-release slot. A dashed ghost arm shows the wrist and finger as dated by the stale edge at t0, with a dashed circle marking the slot tolerance E_max around the finger. The current arm at t0 + Δt shows the wrist shifted laterally by e_trans = v_drift Δt and the link of length ℓ turned by Δθ = ω Δt, which swings the finger by e_rot ≈ ℓ Δθ. A red vector from the stale finger position to the current finger, labeled e_tool ≈ E_0 + e_trans + ℓ Δθ, ends well outside the E_max circle."}
![](images/svg/fig09_frame_staleness_error.svg){width="62%"}
:::

The red vector in @fig-frame-staleness-error crosses the tolerance boundary even though every matrix multiplication remains valid. The worked calculation locates the dominant error in the wrist's lever arm, so increasing timestamp precision alone would not repair the chain. The consumer must compose compatible epochs or reject the expired edge.

::: {#psp-memory-leverage-of-staleness .callout-perspective title="The leverage of staleness"}
*A transform's admissible age is set at the point it serves, not at the joint it measures. The tool point drifts at roughly $v + \ell\omega$, so the longer the lever arm, the sooner an edge expires, and an edge still fresh enough to locate the wrist can be too old to locate the tool center point.*
:::

### Localization drift and map frames that jump {#sec-memory-localization-slam}

The arm's transforms come from encoders that measure every joint. The base has no such anchor. Every map-anchored belief in this chapter, and every row of the stopping budget, inherits the localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, the claim that the machine knows where it stands in its map to within that distance. That claim is produced by two estimators with opposite failure modes, and a memory that stores map cells has to know which one it is leaning on.

**Odometry**\index{Odometry} integrates incremental motion from wheel encoders, the inertial unit, or scan-to-scan lidar matching. It is smooth and fast, but it observes only increments, never absolute position, so the small error in each increment accumulates without bound; position is the unobservable direction of @sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds, here along the aisle. **Map-based localization**\index{Localization!map-based} matches the current scan against a stored map and bounds that error, at the cost of arriving as discrete corrections. **Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)**\index{SLAM}[^fn-slam-landmark-correlation] builds the map while localizing against it. Modern SLAM stores the trajectory as a pose graph, a factor graph whose nodes are past poses and whose factors are odometry and scan-match constraints; when the machine recognizes a place it has visited before, a **loop closure**\index{Loop closure} adds a constraint between the two visits, and re-solving the graph moves past poses to spread the accumulated drift back along the trajectory [@thrun2005probabilistic; @cadena2016past; @dellaert2017factor; @hess2016real]. The filter mechanics that fuse odometry with a correction are those of @sec-perception-state-estimation, with odometry as the prediction step and each map correction as a measurement update, applied late as in @sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation; what matters here is what each estimator does to the age and position of stored evidence.

[^fn-slam-landmark-correlation]: **SLAM**: @smith1990estimating showed that when a moving robot observes landmarks relative to itself, every landmark estimate inherits the common error in the robot's pose, so map error and pose error are correlated and must be estimated together. The acronym came later, in a survey presented at the 1995 International Symposium on Robotics Research [@durrant2006simultaneous]. That correlation is why a loop closure moves remembered cells that no sensor has revisited. \index{SLAM!correlated map and pose error}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-odometry-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ODOMETRY DRIFT AGAINST THE LOCALIZATION BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-localization-slam (where delta_loc comes from).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that odometry alone cannot hold the budget's localization
# │          bound for long, so delta_loc is a premise about how often map
# │          corrections arrive.
# │ Show:    UMBmark return error per meter of path, before and after
# │          calibration; distance and time at the aisle speed before that
# │          rate spends delta_loc; error accumulated over one aisle.
# │ How:     eps = E_max,syst / L_path (L_path = 4 legs x 4 m);
# │          d = delta_loc / eps; t = d / v_aisle; e_aisle = eps * L_aisle.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class OdometryDrift:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (budget localization bound)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (aisle speed)
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative (aisle length)
    # category: literature. Borenstein and Feng (1996), IEEE T-RA 12(6), Secs. 3.3 and 5,
    # Table I, experiment 1 (Fig. 11): TRC LabMate differential-drive base, bidirectional
    # 4 m x 4 m square path at 0.2 m/s with on-the-spot turns; E_max,syst before and after
    # calibration of wheelbase and wheel-diameter ratio; run-to-run std. dev. about 25 mm.
    square_side = 4.0 * ureg.meter  # category: literature (UMBmark leg length)
    n_legs = 4  # category: literature (legs per square run)
    e_uncal = 317.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: literature (E_max,syst, uncalibrated)
    e_cal = 21.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: literature (E_max,syst, calibrated)
    sigma_run = 25.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: literature (return-error std. dev., "about 25 mm")
    v_test = 0.2 * (ureg.meter / ureg.second)  # category: literature (test speed on straight legs)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    path_length = (n_legs * square_side).to(ureg.meter)
    eps_uncal = (e_uncal / path_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    eps_cal = (e_cal / path_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    d_uncal = (delta_loc / eps_uncal).to(ureg.meter)
    d_cal = (delta_loc / eps_cal).to(ureg.meter)
    t_uncal = (d_uncal / v_aisle).to(ureg.second)
    t_cal = (d_cal / v_aisle).to(ureg.second)
    e_aisle_uncal = (eps_uncal * aisle_length).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_aisle_cal = (eps_cal * aisle_length).to(ureg.millimeter)
    aisle_ratio_uncal = (e_aisle_uncal / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    cal_gain = (e_uncal / e_cal).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    speed_ratio = (v_aisle / v_test).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(path_length.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, f"UMBmark path should be 16 m, got {path_length}.")
    check(d_uncal < aisle_length, "Uncalibrated odometry must spend delta_loc within one aisle.")
    check(d_cal > aisle_length, "Calibrated lab odometry holds delta_loc over one aisle, barely.")
    check(d_cal < 2 * aisle_length, "Even calibrated odometry must spend delta_loc within two aisles.")
    check(sigma_run > e_cal, "Run-to-run spread must exceed the calibrated systematic error.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    square_side_str = fmt_length(square_side, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    path_length_str = fmt_length(path_length, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    v_test_str = fmt_velocity(v_test, precision=1)
    e_uncal_str = fmt_length(e_uncal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    e_cal_str = fmt_length(e_cal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_run_str = fmt_length(sigma_run, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_uncal_pct_str = fmt_percent(eps_uncal, precision=1, style="prose")
    eps_cal_pct_str = fmt_percent(eps_cal, precision=2, style="prose")
    cal_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cal_gain, precision=1)
    d_uncal_str = fmt_length(d_uncal, unit=ureg.meter, precision=1)
    t_uncal_str = fmt_latency(t_uncal, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    d_cal_str = fmt_length(d_cal, unit=ureg.meter, precision=1)
    t_cal_str = fmt_latency(t_cal, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    e_aisle_uncal_str = fmt_length(e_aisle_uncal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    e_aisle_cal_str = fmt_length(e_aisle_cal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    aisle_ratio_uncal_mult_str = fmt_multiple(aisle_ratio_uncal, precision=1)
    speed_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speed_ratio, precision=1)
```

A measured number shows why $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ is a premise about corrections rather than a property of the base (@fig-09-odometry-drift). The classic measurement of odometry error is Borenstein and Feng's University of Michigan Benchmark (UMBmark): a differential-drive base drives a `{python} OdometryDrift.square_side_str` square, `{python} OdometryDrift.path_length_str` of travel, five times clockwise and five times counterclockwise, and the benchmark records how far the pose that odometry reports on return lies from the pose an external sensor measures. Its figure of merit is the larger of the two directions' average return errors, which isolates the systematic error from run-to-run scatter. Running both directions separates the two dominant systematic errors, unequal wheel diameters and an uncertain effective wheelbase, which would partly cancel on a single-direction run [@borenstein1996measurement]. On their laboratory base the uncalibrated return error was `{python} OdometryDrift.e_uncal_str`, and after calibrating the wheel-diameter ratio and wheelbase it fell to `{python} OdometryDrift.e_cal_str`, a `{python} OdometryDrift.cal_gain_mult_str` improvement. Dividing by the path length gives about `{python} OdometryDrift.eps_uncal_pct_str` and `{python} OdometryDrift.eps_cal_pct_str` of distance traveled. Charged at the uncalibrated rate, the `{python} OdometryDrift.delta_loc_str` bound is spent after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_uncal_str`, `{python} OdometryDrift.t_uncal_str` at the `{python} OdometryDrift.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, and one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle accumulates `{python} OdometryDrift.e_aisle_uncal_str`, `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_ratio_uncal_mult_str` the bound. Even the calibrated rate spends the bound after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_cal_str`, `{python} OdometryDrift.t_cal_str`, just over one aisle, which on its own accumulates `{python} OdometryDrift.e_aisle_cal_str`.

Three facts make the calibrated figure a best case rather than a design value. The benchmark ran at `{python} OdometryDrift.v_test_str` on its straight legs, slowly enough to avoid wheel slip, and stopped at each corner to turn in place; the loaded base runs `{python} OdometryDrift.speed_ratio_mult_str` faster on a warehouse floor. Calibration removes only the systematic part. The run-to-run spread, a standard deviation of about `{python} OdometryDrift.sigma_run_str`, already exceeds the `{python} OdometryDrift.e_cal_str` that calibration leaves, and that random part keeps growing with distance. Finally, a per-meter rate is a first-order summary. A small heading error $\delta\theta$ displaces the base sideways by about $\delta\theta\,d$ after a straight run of length $d$. Wheel-diameter mismatch makes the heading error itself grow with distance, $\delta\theta \approx \kappa d$ for a heading drift of $\kappa$ radians per meter, so the lateral error grows as about $\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa d^2$ and quadruples each time the straight run doubles. The budget's localization row therefore holds only while map corrections arrive well within one aisle. The site value comes from the same kind of measurement on the deployed base: a ground-truth drive past surveyed markers, at operating speed and payload over the floor conditions the site permits, reporting error per meter at a stated percentile.

::: {#fig-09-odometry-drift fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Odometry drift against the localization bound**: The UMBmark return error, scaled per meter of path, grows linearly with distance driven. Uncalibrated, it spends the `{python} OdometryDrift.delta_loc_str` localization bound after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_uncal_str`; calibrated, after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_cal_str`, only just beyond one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle. Both lines are best cases from a slow laboratory run, so the distance between map corrections, not the base, sets whether $\\delta_{\\text{loc}}$ holds." fig-alt="Line plot of accumulated odometry error in millimeters against distance driven in meters, from 0 to 60 m. A steep line for uncalibrated odometry leaves the top of the plot within a few meters, and a shallow line for calibrated odometry rises slowly. A red dashed horizontal line marks the localization bound, and markers show where each line crosses it. A gray dashed vertical line marks the length of one aisle."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-memory-odometry-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ODOMETRY DRIFT AGAINST THE LOCALIZATION BOUND (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-09-odometry-drift in @sec-memory-localization-slam
# │ Goal:    show that delta_loc is a premise about how often corrections
# │          arrive, not a property of the base
# │ Show:    error vs distance for uncalibrated and calibrated odometry,
# │          the delta_loc line, the crossings, one aisle length
# │ How:     e(d) = eps * d with eps from the OdometryDrift cell
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
OD = OdometryDrift
DLOC = OD.delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (from the cell)
EU, EC = OD.eps_uncal, OD.eps_cal  # category: literature-derived (from the cell)
DU = OD.d_uncal.to(ureg.meter).magnitude
DC = OD.d_cal.to(ureg.meter).magnitude
LA = OD.aisle_length.to(ureg.meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (from the cell)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
d = np.linspace(0, 2 * LA, 400)
check(abs(EU * DU * 1000 - DLOC) < 1e-6 and abs(EC * DC * 1000 - DLOC) < 1e-6, "Crossings must spend delta_loc exactly.")

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.0))
ax.plot(d, EU * d * 1000, color=C["OrangeLine"], lw=1.8, label="uncalibrated odometry")
ax.plot(d, EC * d * 1000, color=C["BlueLine"], lw=1.8, label="calibrated odometry")
ax.axhline(DLOC, color=C["RedLine"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 4)))
ax.text(12, DLOC + 3, rf"localization bound $\delta_{{loc}}$ = {OD.delta_loc_str}", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5, color=C["RedLine"])
ax.axvline(LA, color="#A0AEC0", lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
ax.text(LA + 0.6, 112, f"one aisle, {OD.aisle_length_str}", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7.5, color="#4A5568")
for x, c in ((DU, C["OrangeLine"]), (DC, C["BlueLine"])):
    ax.plot([x], [DLOC], "o", ms=5, color=c, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    OD.d_uncal_str,
    xy=(DU, DLOC),
    xytext=(DU + 3.5, DLOC + 30),
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=C["OrangeLine"],
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.7, color=C["OrangeLine"]),
)
ax.annotate(
    OD.d_cal_str,
    xy=(DC, DLOC),
    xytext=(DC + 3, DLOC - 25),
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=C["BlueLine"],
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.7, color=C["BlueLine"]),
)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2 * LA)
ax.set_ylim(0, 120)
ax.set_xlabel("Distance driven (m)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Odometry error (mm)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.86), fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

Loop closure raises a problem that no single-epoch record anticipates. A map cell stored in the map frame keeps its evidence epoch, because the photons that observed it are exactly as old as they were, yet its position changes when the graph re-solves the pose it hangs from. The cell's evidence is not renewed, and its location is suddenly different. A snapshot copied before the closure therefore places that cell wrong by up to the size of the correction, while every timestamp in it still passes an age check. A map belief must carry the revision of the pose graph that placed it alongside its cell epochs, and a closure that moves the supporting poses must either re-anchor the dependent snapshots or expire them.

The robotics convention for mobile bases, ROS REP 105, separates the two estimators into frames so that consumers can choose the property they need [@meeussen2010rep105]. The `odom` frame carries odometry: the base's pose in it is continuous, never jumping, but drifts without bound. The `map` frame carries localization: the pose in it does not drift significantly, but it can change in discrete jumps whenever a correction or closure arrives. The localizer publishes the `map`-to-`odom` transform, so a correction moves that one edge and leaves the chain from `odom` to `base_link` smooth. The permission controller's local snapshot belongs in the continuous frame. Over the few seconds a snapshot lives, drift in `odom` accumulates slowly and can be charged against $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ from the distance traveled since the snapshot was built, whereas a snapshot held in `map` would see its hull teleport by the size of every correction. Goals, the host map, and snapshot construction stay in `map`; after a correction the host rebuilds the snapshot rather than letting the controller absorb the jump. The `map`-to-`odom` edge is itself a transform with an evidence epoch, and the rules of this section apply to it like any other edge.

A stale transform displaces both the tool estimate and any observations mapped through it. The surrounding world ages too, but it has no joint encoders to report its motion. Memory must therefore record which surfaces and empty regions the sensors actually verified, as well as the frames in which those observations hold.

## Certified Spatial Assertions in Scene Memory {#sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers}

After the robot sweeps its range sensor down an aisle, memory must distinguish space it saw occupied, space it saw empty, and space it never saw. Only observed empty space can support a clearance claim, and only while that evidence remains valid. A map that merges unknown space with free space defeats the evidence-age checks even if every stored timestamp is correct.

The representation must also serve consumers with different needs. A learned policy needs object identity and local geometry to propose a route or grasp. The permission path needs bounded geometric queries whose evidence can be checked before its deadline. Metric maps supply distances and occupancy, scene graphs organize those quantities into objects and places, and episodic memory preserves the interaction history needed to interpret them. These layers share evidence without giving a semantic label or remembered event authority to certify clearance.

### Volumetric metric maps and distance fields {#sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps}

The aisle clearance query asks the map for one quantity, the distance from a body hull to the nearest place that is occupied, unobserved, or no longer vouched for. A rendering query asks for something else, what a camera at a given pose would see. A representation earns a place on the permission path by answering the first question, within the time the permission tick allows, from storage the permission controller actually has. We therefore allocate the query workload first, count what each representation must read to answer it, and only then size the storage.

#### Collision query latency deadlines for reactive safety filters {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-representation-query
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLEARANCE QUERY COST AND LOCAL SNAPSHOT STORAGE BY REPRESENTATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps (query semantics, read budget,
# │          snapshot sizing), @tbl-09-representation-queries,
# │          @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto.
# │
# │ Goal:    Replace stipulated latencies with counts a reader can recompute:
# │          memory reads per sphere-hull clearance query, and the bytes a
# │          local snapshot of the stopping corridor needs.
# │ Show:    the per-query read budget on the permission MCU; reads for a
# │          dense occupancy scan, a worst-case octree scan, and an ESDF
# │          lookup at 2, 5, and 10 cm; snapshot bytes against MCU SRAM.
# │ How:     reads budget = t_query x SRAM bandwidth / cell bytes;
# │          occupancy scan = (4/3) pi ((r_hull + delta_margin) / r)^3 cells;
# │          octree = scan x ceil(log2(L_map / r)) dependent reads;
# │          ESDF = 8 reads (one trilinear lookup); snapshot = V_slab / r^3 x
# │          cell bytes; quantization = (sqrt 3 / 2) r.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_qty_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

def _representation_rows(pitches_cm, reach, l_map, v_slab, s_esdf, s_occ, n_trilinear):
    rows = {}
    for cm in pitches_cm:
        r = cm * ureg.centimeter
        scan = 4 / 3 * math.pi * (reach / r).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude ** 3
        depth = math.ceil(math.log2((l_map / r).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude))
        cells = (v_slab / r**3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
        rows[cm] = dict(
            occ_reads=scan,
            depth=depth,
            oct_reads=scan * depth,
            esdf_reads=n_trilinear,
            esdf_bytes=(cells * s_esdf).to(ureg.kilobyte),
            occ_bytes=(cells * s_occ).to(ureg.kilobyte),
            quant=(math.sqrt(3) / 2 * r).to(ureg.millimeter),
        )
    return rows

class RepresentationQuery:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen (permission-loop rate)
    t_reflex = 100 * microsecond  # category: chosen (collision-check allocation within the permission tick)
    n_hulls = 50  # category: illustrative (sphere hulls covering the machine, worked case)
    n_hulls_min = 20  # category: illustrative (fewest evaluation spheres considered)
    r_hull = 0.25 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (sphere-hull radius)
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen (protective clearance)
    sram_bw = RM.permission_mcu.memory.sram_bandwidth  # category: datasheet (permission MCU SRAM, reference class)
    sram_cap = RM.permission_mcu.memory.sram_capacity  # category: datasheet (permission MCU SRAM, reference class)
    s_esdf = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (4 B distance, 2 B weight, 2 B evidence epoch)
    s_occ = 4 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (2 B log-odds, 2 B evidence epoch)
    l_map = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (host-map edge, the 10 m workcell below)
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative (aisle width)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (clear distance ahead)
    h_slab = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (snapshot height covering the arm's reach)
    pitches_cm = (2, 5, 10)  # category: chosen (voxel pitches compared)
    n_trilinear = 8  # category: derived (corner cells of one trilinear interpolation)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_tick = (1 / f_tick).to(microsecond)
    frac_spare = 1 - (t_reflex / t_tick).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude  # tick left for other permission work
    t_query = (t_reflex / n_hulls).to(microsecond)
    reads_budget = (t_query * sram_bw / s_esdf).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    reach = (r_hull + delta_margin).to(ureg.meter)
    v_slab = (aisle_width * d_clear * h_slab).to(ureg.meter**3)
    rows = _representation_rows(pitches_cm, reach, l_map, v_slab, s_esdf, s_occ, n_trilinear)
    r2, r5, r10 = rows[2], rows[5], rows[10]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_query.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Per-query allocation should be 2 us, got {t_query}.")
    check(abs(frac_spare - 0.90) < 1e-9, f"The allocation should leave 90 percent of the tick, got {frac_spare}.")
    check(n_hulls_min < n_hulls, "The hull range must be ordered.")
    check(abs(reads_budget - 800) < 1e-6, f"Read budget should be 800 cells, got {reads_budget}.")
    check(r5["occ_reads"] > reads_budget > r10["occ_reads"], "An occupancy scan must fit only at the coarsest pitch.")
    check(r10["oct_reads"] > reads_budget, "A worst-case octree scan must miss the budget at every pitch.")
    check(n_trilinear < reads_budget, "An ESDF lookup must fit at every pitch.")
    check(r5["esdf_bytes"] < sram_cap < r2["esdf_bytes"], "The 5 cm snapshot must fit SRAM and the 2 cm one must not.")
    check(r10["quant"] > delta_margin / 2, "At 10 cm, quantization alone must exceed half the protective clearance.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_query_str = fmt_latency(t_query, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    f_tick_str = fmt_frequency(f_tick, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=microsecond, precision=0, commas=True)
    t_reflex_str = fmt_latency(t_reflex, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    n_hulls_str = fmt_int(n_hulls)
    n_hulls_min_str = fmt_int(n_hulls_min)
    frac_spare_pct_str = fmt_percent(frac_spare, precision=0, style="prose")
    sram_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(sram_bw, precision=1)
    sram_cap_str = fmt_memory(sram_cap, unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=2)
    reads_budget_str = fmt_int(reads_budget)
    r_hull_str = fmt_length(r_hull, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    reach_str = fmt_length(reach, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    v_slab_str = fmt_qty(v_slab, ureg.meter**3, precision=2)
    h_slab_str = fmt_length(h_slab, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    occ2_str, occ5_str, occ10_str = (fmt_int(r["occ_reads"]) for r in (r2, r5, r10))
    oct2_str, oct5_str, oct10_str = (fmt_int(r["oct_reads"]) for r in (r2, r5, r10))
    depth5_str = fmt_int(r5["depth"])
    esdf_reads_str = fmt_int(n_trilinear)
    esdf2_bytes_str = fmt_memory(r2["esdf_bytes"], unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=2)
    esdf5_bytes_str = fmt_qty_int(r5["esdf_bytes"], ureg.kilobyte)
    esdf10_bytes_str = fmt_memory(r10["esdf_bytes"], unit=ureg.kilobyte, precision=1)
    quant5_str = fmt_qty_int(r5["quant"], ureg.millimeter)
    quant10_str = fmt_qty_int(r10["quant"], ureg.millimeter)
```

The worked design allocates spatial collision checking within the machine's `{python} RepresentationQuery.f_tick_str` permission loop ($T_{\text{tick}} =$ `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_tick_str`). The required query returns conservative clearance at each body collision hull; where the selected filter needs a gradient, that work belongs in the same measured query. For an illustrative `{python} RepresentationQuery.n_hulls_min_str` to `{python} RepresentationQuery.n_hulls_str` evaluation spheres, the total work is:
$$T_{\text{query\_total}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{hulls}}} t_{\text{query}}(\mathbf{x}_k) \le T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}$$ {#eq-mem-query-latency-budget}
To bound the total collision workload in @eq-mem-query-latency-budget, the worked $N_{\text{hulls}} =$ `{python} RepresentationQuery.n_hulls_str` case reserves $T_{\text{reflex\_budget}} =$ `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_reflex_str` for local collision checking, leaving `{python} RepresentationQuery.frac_spare_pct_str` of the tick for the other permission and communication work. This is an allocation to be tested on the deployed controller; full-map updates and trajectory optimization run outside this tick. Dividing the allocation among the hulls gives
$$t_{\text{query}} \le \frac{T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}}{N_{\text{hulls}}},$$
which for the worked case is `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_reflex_str` over `{python} RepresentationQuery.n_hulls_str` hulls, or `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str` per query.


A time allocation becomes a design constraint once it is expressed in the unit the hardware spends, memory reads. The permission controller streams its local SRAM at `{python} RepresentationQuery.sram_bw_str`, so the `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str` allocation covers at most `{python} RepresentationQuery.reads_budget_str` reads of an 8-byte cell per hull query, before any arithmetic, cache effect, or contention; qualification on the deployed controller must still measure the real bound (@sec-placement). Against that ceiling, the representations differ less in speed than in which question one read answers (@tbl-09-representation-queries). An **occupancy grid**\index{Occupancy grid}[^fn-occupancy-grid-sonar] stores, per cell, whether that cell is occupied [@elfes1989using; @moravec1985high]; certifying that a sphere hull of radius `{python} RepresentationQuery.r_hull_str` keeps its protective clearance means reading every cell within `{python} RepresentationQuery.reach_str` of its center, $\frac{4}{3}\pi\left((r_{\text{hull}}+\delta_{\text{margin}})/r\right)^3$ cells at pitch $r$. A hierarchical **octree** such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap] answers the same point query after descending the tree, one dependent read per level, so near surfaces, where pruning cannot merge cells, the scan costs its cell count times the tree depth. A **truncated signed distance field (TSDF)**\index{Truncated signed distance field} stores the distance to the nearest surface along the sensor ray, clamped at a truncation distance of a few voxels [@curless1996volumetric]; one read answers only whether a surface lies within that truncation, so "farther than the truncation" never certifies a clearance larger than it. A **Euclidean signed distance field (ESDF)**\index{Euclidean signed distance field} stores the straight-line distance to the nearest obstacle [@oleynikova2017voxblox; @millane2024nvblox], so one interpolated lookup, `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` corner reads, certifies clearance for an entire sphere: the hull passes when the distance at its center exceeds $r_{\text{hull}} + \delta_{\text{margin}}$ plus the geometric error. Rendering representations answer the second question. A 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) scene fits anisotropic Gaussians to a photometric loss [@kerbl20233d], and a neural radiance field integrates learned density along camera rays; neither stores a conservative distance, and collision checking on splats requires an added assumption that the fitted ellipsoids enclose the physical surface [@chen2025splatnav]. Their parameterizations are collected in @sec-appendix-ml-3dgs, and the occupancy and TSDF update equations in @sec-appendix-ml-voxels.

[^fn-occupancy-grid-sonar]: **Occupancy Grid**: Moravec and Elfes built the first grids at Carnegie Mellon to fuse returns from wide-beam sonar, whose single echo cannot say where across its beam the reflector lies [@moravec1985high]. Each cell therefore holds accumulated evidence rather than geometry, and a cell no return has reached stays at its prior. The representation was designed for sensors too coarse to vouch for what they did not touch, which is why a permission-grade grid must keep unknown distinct from free. \index{Occupancy grid!sonar origin}

| Representation         | Query one lookup answers                      |                  Reads per hull query at 5 cm | Can certify the hull's clearance?                        |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Dense occupancy grid   | Is this cell occupied?                        |       `{python} RepresentationQuery.occ5_str` | Yes, by scanning every cell within reach                 |
| Octree occupancy       | Is this cell occupied? (after a tree descent) |       `{python} RepresentationQuery.oct5_str` | Yes, by the same scan, one descent per cell              |
| TSDF                   | Is a surface within the truncation distance?  |                                             1 | Only up to the truncation distance                       |
| ESDF                   | How far is the nearest obstacle?              | `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` | Yes, with unknown cells treated as obstacles             |
| 3DGS or radiance field | What would a camera at this pose see?         |                                             — | No; requires a separately qualified geometric conversion |

: **What one lookup answers, and what clearance costs**: Reads for a sphere hull of radius `{python} RepresentationQuery.r_hull_str` plus the protective clearance, at a 5 cm pitch, against a budget of `{python} RepresentationQuery.reads_budget_str` reads per query on the permission controller. The octree count is the worst case near surfaces, a tree depth of `{python} RepresentationQuery.depth5_str` levels per cell; pruning reduces it in open space. {#tbl-09-representation-queries tbl-colwidths="[20,32,16,32]"}

::: {#fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Clearance query cost and snapshot storage by representation family**: (a) Memory reads to certify one sphere hull's clearance, computed from voxel pitch, hull radius plus protective clearance, and tree depth, against the per-query read budget that the 2 µs allocation and the permission controller's SRAM bandwidth allow. Occupancy scans grow with the cube of the inverse pitch and fit only at the coarsest pitch; an ESDF answers with one interpolated lookup at every pitch. (b) Storage for a dense snapshot of the stopping corridor (aisle width by clear distance by a chosen 2 m height) against the controller's SRAM. Counts, not measured latencies; rendering representations are absent because they do not answer a clearance query." fig-alt="Two log-scale panels against voxel pitch of 2, 5, and 10 cm. Panel a, memory reads per sphere-hull clearance query: worst-case octree scan from about 200,000 to about 1,300 reads, dense occupancy scan from about 22,000 to 180 reads, and ESDF lookup flat at 8 reads, with a dashed red read budget at 800 per query, shaded above, that only the ESDF clears at every pitch and the occupancy scan clears only at 10 cm. Panel b, snapshot storage in kilobytes: ESDF at 8 bytes per cell falls from about 2,900 kB to 23 kB and occupancy at 4 bytes per cell from about 1,400 kB to 11 kB, with a dashed red line at the permission MCU SRAM of about 1 MB, shaded above, that both snapshots exceed at 2 cm and fit under at 5 and 10 cm."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-memory-representation-pareto
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLEARANCE QUERY COST AND SNAPSHOT STORAGE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto
# │ Goal:    show which representation answers a sphere-hull clearance query
# │          inside the per-query read budget, and which pitch fits the
# │          permission MCU's SRAM
# │ Show:    reads per query vs pitch (occupancy scan, octree scan, ESDF);
# │          snapshot storage vs pitch against SRAM capacity
# │ How:     all values from the RepresentationQuery cell
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
RQ = RepresentationQuery
PITCH = list(RQ.pitches_cm)  # cm, category: chosen (as in the cell)
OCC = [RQ.rows[p]["occ_reads"] for p in PITCH]
OCT = [RQ.rows[p]["oct_reads"] for p in PITCH]
ESDF = [RQ.rows[p]["esdf_reads"] for p in PITCH]
ESDF_KB = [RQ.rows[p]["esdf_bytes"].to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude for p in PITCH]
OCC_KB = [RQ.rows[p]["occ_bytes"].to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude for p in PITCH]
BUDGET = RQ.reads_budget
SRAM_KB = RQ.sram_cap.to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude

# ┌── 2. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
FS = 7.5

ax1.plot(PITCH, OCT, marker="s", ms=4, lw=1.6, color=C["OrangeLine"], label="octree occupancy scan (worst case)")
ax1.plot(PITCH, OCC, marker="o", ms=4, lw=1.6, color=C["primary"], label="dense occupancy scan")
ax1.plot(PITCH, ESDF, marker="^", ms=4, lw=1.6, color=C["BlueLine"], label="ESDF lookup (trilinear)")
ax1.axhline(BUDGET, color=C["RedLine"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 4)))
ax1.axhspan(BUDGET, 3e6, color=C["RedFill"], alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax1.text(1.7, BUDGET * 0.6, f"read budget: {BUDGET:.0f} per query", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=FS, color=C["RedLine"])
ax1.set_yscale("log")
ax1.set_xticks(PITCH)
ax1.set_xlim(1.5, 10.5)
ax1.set_ylim(3, 3e6)
ax1.set_xlabel("Voxel pitch (cm)", fontsize=8)
ax1.set_ylabel("Memory reads per sphere-hull query", fontsize=8)
ax1.set_title("(a) Clearance query cost", loc="left", fontsize=9)
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=6.5)
ax1.tick_params(labelsize=FS)

ax2.plot(PITCH, ESDF_KB, marker="^", ms=4, lw=1.6, color=C["BlueLine"], label="ESDF snapshot, 8 B per cell")
ax2.plot(PITCH, OCC_KB, marker="o", ms=4, lw=1.6, color=C["primary"], ls=(0, (6, 3)), label="occupancy snapshot, 4 B per cell")
ax2.axhline(SRAM_KB, color=C["RedLine"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 4)))
ax2.axhspan(SRAM_KB, 6e4, color=C["RedFill"], alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax2.text(10.1, SRAM_KB * 1.25, "permission MCU SRAM", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=FS, color=C["RedLine"])
ax2.set_yscale("log")
ax2.set_xticks(PITCH)
ax2.set_xlim(1.5, 10.5)
ax2.set_ylim(5, 6e4)
ax2.set_xlabel("Voxel pitch (cm)", fontsize=8)
ax2.set_ylabel("Snapshot storage (kB)", fontsize=8)
ax2.set_title("(b) Stopping-corridor snapshot", loc="left", fontsize=9)

plt.show()
```

:::

The counts in @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto make the choice without any stipulated latency. A dense occupancy scan misses the read budget at 2 and 5 cm and fits only at 10 cm, where quantization alone, up to half a cell diagonal or `{python} RepresentationQuery.quant10_str`, consumes most of the protective clearance. A worst-case octree scan misses at every pitch, because each cell costs a descent. The ESDF answers with the same `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` reads at every pitch, which is why it is the local snapshot's representation: its per-query cost does not grow as the pitch shrinks, and its storage becomes the binding constraint instead. A dense ESDF snapshot of the stopping corridor, the aisle width by the clear distance by a chosen `{python} RepresentationQuery.h_slab_str` height, or `{python} RepresentationQuery.v_slab_str`, needs `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf5_bytes_str` at 5 cm and fits the controller's `{python} RepresentationQuery.sram_cap_str` of SRAM, while at 2 cm it needs `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf2_bytes_str` and does not. The 5 cm pitch then charges up to `{python} RepresentationQuery.quant5_str` of quantization to the geometric error of every lookup, a cost the clearance check must subtract. A TSDF's projective distance cannot substitute for Euclidean clearance merely because its lookup is cheap.

The host maintains the larger reconstruction and prepares a bounded region covering the admitted motion and its fallback. The permission controller accepts a snapshot only when its provenance, geometry bounds, per-region evidence ages, and coverage satisfy the qualified interface. Snapshot construction, transfer, and admission consume time and memory of their own; @sec-placement must place and qualify that work separately from the local query. If the host stalls, the existing snapshot keeps aging. Motion can continue only while its own evidence, coverage, and fallback remain valid.

#### Volumetric memory footprint scaling {.unnumbered}

The local decision leaves the host with a capacity and update problem. Keeping the chosen snapshot supplied requires enough memory for the underlying map and enough bandwidth to integrate observations before their evidence expires.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-hashed-voxel-payload
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE HOST MAP SIZING: DENSE GRID VERSUS HASHED NARROW BAND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps, host capacity calculation.
# │
# │ Goal:    Separate a dense workcell grid from a hashed surface band, and
# │          voxel payload from total allocated storage.
# │ Show:    dense grid bytes; band volume; block count; hashed payload.
# │ How:     M_dense = V / r^3 x S; V_band = 2 delta A; N_blocks = V_band /
# │          (B r)^3; payload = N_blocks x B^3 x S.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_memory, fmt_qty, fmt_qty_int, fmt_sci, sci_latex, check

class HashedVoxelPayload:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    l_x = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell length)
    l_y = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell width)
    l_z = 3.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell height)
    pitch = 0.01 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (manipulation resolution)
    voxel_bytes = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (distance, weight, epoch payload)
    a_surface = 120.0 * ureg.meter**2  # category: illustrative (obstacle surface area in the workcell)
    delta_band = 0.04 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (truncation band half-width)
    block_side = 8  # category: illustrative (voxels per block edge, the nvblox layout)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_ws = (l_x * l_y * l_z).to(ureg.meter**3)
    n_dense = (v_ws / pitch**3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    m_dense = (n_dense * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.gigabyte)
    v_band = (2 * delta_band * a_surface).to(ureg.meter**3)
    blocks = (v_band / (block_side * pitch) ** 3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    payload = (blocks * block_side**3 * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.megabyte)
    block_bytes = (block_side**3 * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.byte)
    band_fraction = (v_band / v_ws).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_dense.magnitude - 2.4) < 1e-9, f"Dense grid should be 2.4 GB, got {m_dense}.")
    check(abs(v_band.magnitude - 9.6) < 1e-9, f"Band volume should be 9.6 m^3, got {v_band}.")
    check(abs(blocks - 18_750) < 1e-6, f"Block count should be 18,750, got {blocks}.")
    check(abs(payload.magnitude - 76.8) < 1e-9, "Voxel payload is 76.8 MB before overhead.")
    check(abs(block_bytes.magnitude - 4096) < 1e-9, "One 8^3 block of 8 B voxels is 4,096 B.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_ws_str = fmt_qty_int(v_ws, ureg.meter**3)
    pitch_str = fmt_length(pitch, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    voxel_bytes_str = fmt_int(voxel_bytes.magnitude)
    n_dense_str = fmt_sci(n_dense, precision=0)
    m_dense_str = fmt_memory(m_dense, unit=ureg.gigabyte, precision=1)
    a_surface_str = fmt_qty_int(a_surface, ureg.meter**2)
    delta_band_str = fmt_length(delta_band, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    v_band_str = fmt_qty(v_band, ureg.meter**3, precision=1)
    blocks_str = fmt_int(blocks)
    payload_str = fmt_memory(payload, unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=1)
    block_bytes_str = fmt_int(block_bytes.magnitude)
    band_pct_str = fmt_percent(band_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")

    # visible arithmetic for notebook nbk-memory-empty-air-tax
    ratio = (m_dense / payload).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    ratio_str = fmt_int(ratio)
    empty_pct_str = fmt_percent(1 - band_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
    l_x_str = fmt_qty_int(l_x, ureg.meter)
    l_y_str = fmt_qty_int(l_y, ureg.meter)
    l_z_str = fmt_qty_int(l_z, ureg.meter)
    _m = lambda q, p=2: fmt_magnitude(q, ureg.meter, precision=p)
    dense_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{dense}}}} = \frac{{{fmt_magnitude(v_ws, ureg.meter**3, precision=0)}\ \text{{m}}^3}}{{({_m(pitch)}\ \text{{m}})^3}} \times {fmt_int(voxel_bytes.magnitude)}\ \text{{B}} = {sci_latex(n_dense, precision=0)} \times {fmt_int(voxel_bytes.magnitude)}\ \text{{B}} = {fmt_magnitude(m_dense, ureg.gigabyte, precision=1)}\ \text{{GB}}"
    )
    band_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"V_{{\text{{band}}}} = 2 \times {_m(delta_band)}\ \text{{m}} \times {fmt_magnitude(a_surface, ureg.meter**2, precision=0)}\ \text{{m}}^2 = {fmt_magnitude(v_band, ureg.meter**3, precision=1)}\ \text{{m}}^3"
    )
    hashed_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"N_{{\text{{blocks}}}} = \frac{{{fmt_magnitude(v_band, ureg.meter**3, precision=1)}\ \text{{m}}^3}}{{({block_side} \times {_m(pitch)}\ \text{{m}})^3}} = \text{{{fmt_int(blocks)}}}, \qquad \text{{{fmt_int(blocks)}}} \times {block_side}^3 \times {fmt_int(voxel_bytes.magnitude)}\ \text{{B}} = {fmt_magnitude(payload, ureg.megabyte, precision=1)}\ \text{{MB}}"
    )
    check(30 < ratio < 32, f"Dense-to-hashed payload ratio should be about 31x, got {ratio}.")
```

For the illustrative host-map sizing calculation, consider an operational workspace of physical volume $V_{\text{ws}} = L_x L_y L_z$. Discretizing this domain into cubic voxels of uniform pitch $r$ requires memory proportional to workspace volume and to the inverse cube of voxel width:
$$M_{\text{dense}} = \left(\frac{V_{\text{ws}}}{r^3}\right) S_{\text{voxel}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-dense}
where $S_{\text{voxel}}$ represents the storage footprint per voxel, here `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.voxel_bytes_str` bytes: 4 for a 32-bit distance, 2 for the observation weight, and 2 for the evidence epoch.

Obstacles occupy thin surfaces, not volumes, and a TSDF[^fn-tsdf-truncation-distance] needs values only near them. Truncating the distance field to a band $[-\delta, +\delta]$ around observed surfaces restricts storage to a shell $V_{\text{band}} \approx 2\delta \cdot A_{\text{surface}}$, where $A_{\text{surface}}$ is the total obstacle surface area. Partitioning space into blocks of $B^3$ voxels with block pitch $L_B = B \cdot r$, and allocating a block only when it holds data, the sparse hashed footprint obeys:
$$M_{\text{hashed}} = N_{\text{blocks}} \left( B^3 S_{\text{voxel}} + S_{\text{meta}} \right) + N_{\text{buckets}} S_{\text{entry}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-hashed}
where $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx \lceil 2\delta A_{\text{surface}} / (B r)^3 \rceil$, $S_{\text{meta}}$ is the block metadata (coordinates, allocation flags), and $S_{\text{entry}}$ is the hash-table entry size. Notebook \ref{nbk-memory-empty-air-tax} applies both equations to one warehouse workcell.

::: {#nbk-memory-empty-air-tax .callout-notebook title="The empty-air tax"}

**Problem**: A host map must cover a warehouse workcell of `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.l_x_str` by `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.l_y_str` by `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.l_z_str` at the resolution manipulation needs. How much memory does a dense grid take, how much does a hashed band around the obstacle surfaces take, and what fraction of the dense grid describes empty air?

**Variables**:

* Workcell volume $V_{\text{ws}} =$ `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.v_ws_str` (illustrative) at pitch $r =$ `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.pitch_str` (chosen), with $S_{\text{voxel}} =$ `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.voxel_bytes_str` B per voxel (illustrative).
* Obstacle surface $A_{\text{surface}} =$ `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.a_surface_str` (illustrative) and band half-width $\delta =$ `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.delta_band_str` (chosen).
* Block edge $B = 8$ voxels, the nvblox layout (datasheet).

**Math**: The dense grid, by @eq-mem-footprint-dense:
`{python} HashedVoxelPayload.dense_math`
The band and its voxel payload, by @eq-mem-footprint-hashed without metadata or hash entries:
`{python} HashedVoxelPayload.band_math`
`{python} HashedVoxelPayload.hashed_math`

**Result**: The dense grid needs `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.m_dense_str` for `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.n_dense_str` voxels. The band is `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.band_pct_str` of the workcell, so `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.empty_pct_str` of the dense grid describes space with no surface in it, and the hashed payload of `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.payload_str` in `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.blocks_str` blocks is about `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.ratio_str` times smaller.

**Systems insight**: Obstacles are surfaces, not volumes, so a dense grid pays mostly for empty air, and on an embedded robot computer that allocation competes with the vision backbone and the controllers. The hashed figure is a lower bound, because block metadata, hash entries, and the partly filled blocks at band boundaries add to it, and the saving belongs to the TSDF alone.

:::

[^fn-tsdf-truncation-distance]: **Truncated Signed Distance Field**: @curless1996volumetric averaged many range scans into a signed distance stored only near the surface to build detailed models of real objects, and KinectFusion ran the same fusion in real time on a GPU from a handheld depth camera [@newcombe2011kinectfusion]. Truncation bought both systems their memory savings. It makes the TSDF a representation for reconstructing surfaces, not for certifying the empty space between them. \index{Truncated signed distance field!origin}

The narrow-band estimate describes a TSDF, not the ESDF the snapshot needs. An ESDF stores a distance wherever a clearance may be queried, which means over the observed free volume out to its maximum distance, so its footprint scales with $V_{\text{obs}}/r^3$ rather than with surface area; for an aisle machine that volume is the corridor the machine can reach, which is why the snapshot above was sized from the corridor. Allocation also carries meaning. When ray integration allocates every block a sensor ray crosses, as free-space carving does, an unallocated block is one no ray has reached and can be read as unknown. When only the surface band is allocated, an unallocated block may be observed free space, and the map must mark observation separately. A permission-grade map therefore distinguishes three states explicitly rather than inferring them from allocation: observed free with a live evidence epoch, unknown, and expired, meaning observed once but older than its horizon.

#### Voxel block hashing index mapping {.unnumbered}

Sparse allocation needs an index that finds a block without the pointer chains of an octree. **Voxel block hashing**\index{Voxel block hashing} maps continuous world coordinates $\mathbf{x} = [x, y, z]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to an integer block index $\mathbf{u} = [u_x, u_y, u_z]^\top \in \mathbb{Z}^3$:
$$\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x}}{B \cdot r} \right\rfloor$$ {#eq-mem-block-index}
and a spatial hash then resolves the index of @eq-mem-block-index to a table bucket $h(\mathbf{u}) \in \{0, \dots, N_{\text{buckets}}-1\}$.[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing] The scheme was introduced for large-scale real-time reconstruction by @niessner2013real, using the spatial hash of @teschner2003optimized, and it underlies robotic mapping libraries such as Voxblox and nvblox [@oleynikova2017voxblox; @millane2024nvblox]. In the nvblox layout of $8^3$ voxels per block, an 8-byte voxel makes each block `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.block_bytes_str` bytes laid out contiguously, so one hash lookup brings a whole neighborhood into the same memory region. Retrieval is expected $O(1)$, but hash collisions, probe length, cold caches, and concurrent updates all lengthen the worst case, so expected complexity cannot replace a measured bound for the local permission query; the snapshot above avoids the question by being dense.

[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing]: **Spatial hashing and voxel offsets**\index{Voxel block hashing!spatial hash}: The hash of @teschner2003optimized, adopted by @niessner2013real, computes $h(\mathbf{u}) = (u_x p_1 \oplus u_y p_2 \oplus u_z p_3) \bmod N_{\text{buckets}}$ with the primes $p_1 = 73{,}856{,}093$, $p_2 = 19{,}349{,}663$, and $p_3 = 83{,}492{,}791$. Implementations differ; Voxblox, for example, uses a linear combination of the block coordinates instead. Within a block, the voxel offset is $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \lfloor \mathbf{x}/r \rfloor - B \mathbf{u}$, stored linearly at $\Delta u_x + B(\Delta u_y + B\,\Delta u_z)$.

#### Ray-marching update traffic and negative evidence {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-raymarch-bandwidth
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAIVE RAY-MARCHING UPDATE TRAFFIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps (@eq-mem-dram-bandwidth).
# │
# │ Goal:    Price one depth stream's naive map-update traffic and compare it
# │          with the host SoC's registered peak DRAM bandwidth.
# │ Show:    rays per frame, steps per ray, traffic, share of peak.
# │ How:     BW = f_cam x N_rays x (d_ray / r) x S_rw.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class RaymarchBandwidth:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    width_px = 640  # category: illustrative (VGA depth stream)
    height_px = 480  # category: illustrative (VGA depth stream)
    f_cam = 30 * ureg.hertz  # category: illustrative (depth frame rate)
    d_ray = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (mean marched distance)
    pitch = 0.02 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (voxel pitch)
    s_rw = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (read-modify-write traffic per voxel, low end)
    soc_bw = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (host SoC peak DRAM bandwidth)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_rays = width_px * height_px
    n_steps = (d_ray / pitch).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    bw = (f_cam * n_rays * n_steps * s_rw).to(ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second)
    share = (bw / soc_bw).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(bw.magnitude - 7.3728) < 1e-6, f"Ray-march traffic should be 7.37 GB/s, got {bw}.")
    check(share < 0.05, "One naive depth stream should take under 5 percent of peak.")
    # margin_volumetric_raycasting_bandwidth_ladder.svg draws 204 GB/s, 7.37 GB/s, and 3.6%
    check(abs(soc_bw.to(ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second).magnitude - 204.0) < 1e-9, "Margin figure peak label (204 GB/s) is stale.")
    check(abs(share - 0.036) < 5e-4, "Margin figure share label (3.6%) is stale.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_rays_str = fmt_int(n_rays)
    f_cam_str = fmt_qty_int(f_cam, ureg.hertz)
    d_ray_str = fmt_length(d_ray, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    pitch_str = fmt_length(pitch, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    n_steps_str = fmt_int(n_steps)
    bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw, unit=ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second, precision=2)
    soc_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(soc_bw, unit=ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second, precision=0)
    share_str = fmt_percent(share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

When depth cameras stream range frames at framerate $f_{\text{cam}}$ with $N_{\text{rays}} = W \times H$ pixels per frame, updating the volumetric map requires ray marching from the sensor origin to each observed surface point [@curless1996volumetric]. Each ray traverses a line-of-sight distance $d_{\text{ray}}$ at voxel stepping pitch $r$, requiring $N_{\text{steps}} = d_{\text{ray}} / r$ discrete cell evaluations. The raw DRAM update bandwidth consumed by naive ray marching is:
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = f_{\text{cam}} \cdot N_{\text{rays}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{\text{ray}}}{r}\right) \cdot S_{\text{rw}}$$ {#eq-mem-dram-bandwidth}
where $S_{\text{rw}}$ is the read-modify-write memory traffic per traversed voxel (8 to 16 bytes for reading the current occupancy or distance, updating running weights, and writing back).

For an illustrative VGA depth stream of `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.n_rays_str` rays at `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.f_cam_str`, marched over `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.d_ray_str` at a `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.pitch_str` pitch (`{python} RaymarchBandwidth.n_steps_str` steps per ray) with 8 bytes per step, @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth gives `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.bw_str`, `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.share_str` of the peak `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.soc_bw_str` of the host system-on-chip (SoC). The share of peak understates the effect, because these map updates share the memory system with the vision model and other workloads, and their cost depends on access locality and competing traffic rather than on peak bandwidth. The update calculation identifies a load to include in the contention test; it does not establish a measured interference bound. Block hashing reduces this traffic by keeping active blocks in on-chip memory, and projective TSDF updates project voxels inside the viewing frustum onto the depth image instead of marching every ray. These methods reduce repeated memory traffic, but the reduction depends on scene coverage and update strategy. Sparse allocation still grows as the machine explores new regions; a bounded host store needs an explicit retention policy.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_volumetric_raycasting_bandwidth_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars on a linear scale. An outlined bar reaching a red limit line is labeled SoC peak 204 GB/s. A short blue bar beneath it is labeled ray-march updates, 7.37 GB/s, 3.6 percent."}
*One naive depth stream's ray-march updates take a small share of peak DRAM bandwidth; the share is a load to include in the contention test, not an interference bound.*
:::

What a map can certify comes from how a range return updates it. Traversing the ray[^fn-voxel-ray-traversal] from the sensor to the return [@amanatides1987fast], the map asserts **negative evidence**\index{Negative evidence} in every cell the ray crossed and positive evidence in the cell where it ended; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels gives the log-odds update.[^fn-logodds-unknown-prior] A valid empty ray can retire a phantom obstacle, but it says nothing about the volume behind a return. A new scan down the aisle therefore cannot renew cells hidden behind the rack. Sparse allocation saves capacity without eliminating ray traversal, and any resulting processing delay adds to evidence age (@sec-placement-resource-contention).

[^fn-voxel-ray-traversal]: **Voxel Traversal**: @amanatides1987fast step a ray from one voxel boundary to the next by comparing the distances to the next crossing on each axis and adding one fixed increment, so each voxel visited costs a few comparisons and one addition. The work per ray is therefore proportional to the number of voxels it crosses, range divided by pitch, which is the $d_{\text{ray}}/r$ factor of @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth. \index{Voxel traversal!Amanatides-Woo}

[^fn-logodds-unknown-prior]: **Log-Odds**: Storing $\ell = \ln\big(p/(1-p)\big)$ turns each Bayesian occupancy update into an addition, with an uninformed prior at $\ell = 0$. A cell no ray has touched and a cell that received as many hits as misses both read $\ell = 0$, so the value alone cannot separate never observed from observed and ambiguous. That is why the manifest of @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief carries an explicit `cell_state`. \index{Log-odds!unknown state}

::: {#fig-09-ray-update-epochs fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**One range return updates only the cells it touched**: The cells the ray crosses become free and take the capture epoch $t_1$ of the return, which also retires a phantom obstacle left on that line; the cell holding the return becomes occupied at $t_1$. Cells behind the return and every cell off the ray keep whatever epoch their own last evidence gave them, here $t_0$, so the map's publication time dates none of them." fig-alt="A grid of square cells with a sensor at the left. An arrow runs from the sensor along one row of cells, which are tinted and labeled t1. One of them holds a dashed square labeled phantom retired. The arrow ends at a black cell labeled return, occupied, t1. The four cells beyond it in the same row are hatched and labeled t0, with a note reading behind return, not renewed. The other rows are blank."}
![](images/svg/fig09_ray_update_cell_epochs.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Because negative evidence renews only the cells a ray crossed (@fig-09-ray-update-epochs), a map's publication time dates none of its cells. The manifest in @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief therefore carries cell evidence epochs alongside occupancy. For the worked local snapshot, checking a hull includes the supporting cells' evidence and unknown-space status within the allocated query time. A freshly copied distance value with expired source cells cannot establish clearance. The manifest travels with the bounded snapshot as well as the host map; the isolated controller does not traverse the full host store.

| Map field                                 | Unit or type                         | Meaning and consumer check                                                                                          |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `voxel_grid_origin`, `voxel_resolution_m` | m; m                                 | Spatial anchor and pitch; match the active frame and calibration                                                    |
| `pose_graph_revision`                     | integer                              | Revision of the pose graph that placed the cells; a loop closure that changes it re-anchors or expires the snapshot |
| `map_update_epoch`                        | capture-clock ns                     | Last map publication/update; **not** freshness of every cell                                                        |
| `cell_evidence_epoch`                     | capture-clock ns per cell            | Last physical observation for that cell; never refreshed by prediction or unrelated map updates                     |
| `free_space_sweep_epoch`                  | capture-clock ns per occupancy cell  | Last valid observed free ray through that cell                                                                      |
| `cell_state`                              | free, unknown, or expired per cell   | Set explicitly, never inferred from allocation; unknown and expired read as obstacles                               |
| `clock_conversion`, `sync_error_ns`       | mapping; ns                          | Convert capture epochs to the consumer's monotonic clock with bounded error                                         |
| `query_latency_budget_us`                 | $\mu\text{s}$ (at most `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str`) | Bound collision and distance gradient query time to preserve the `{python} RepresentationQuery.f_tick_str` permission loop                           |

: **Volumetric belief manifest and cell evidence**: The map header describes layout, pose-graph revision, query latency budget, and update time, while cell-local acquisition epochs and states determine whether the particular path region is fresh. The consumer treats unobserved or expired cells as unknown unless a separately validated policy permits traversal. {#tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief tbl-colwidths="[26,22,52]"}

These pieces combine into the one quantity the permission path needs from a map. Build the snapshot ESDF with every occupied, unknown, or expired cell treated as an obstacle. Its value at a hull center, minus the hull radius, is then the **free-space depth**\index{Free-space depth} $d_{\text{free}}$: the distance from the hull's surface to the nearest place that no live evidence vouches for. A person, a tote, or anything else the sensors cannot currently see can only be beyond that boundary, so $d_{\text{free}}$ is exactly what motion may spend. For a candidate aisle advance, the consumer subtracts the geometric error, including quantization and localization, and the protective clearance from $d_{\text{free}}$; if the remainder is positive the query passes. When the nearest boundary is the occluded cross aisle, $d_{\text{free}}$ is small however fast the lookup, and a small numerical query latency cannot rescue the claim. How quickly the remainder shrinks while the sensors cannot see that boundary is the subject of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.

#### Map maintenance: Forgetting, decay, and change {.unnumbered}

A map built for a warehouse must also forget. Totes move, doors swing, and people walk through cells the sensors saw empty a minute ago, so a map that keeps every observation forever accumulates phantom obstacles where objects left and phantom free space where they arrived unseen. Negative evidence handles the first case whenever a ray passes through the cell again. The second case has no ray to correct it, and the practical mechanisms differ in what they assume about the cells nobody is looking at.

@Tbl-09-map-maintenance sets out the mechanisms in current use. Two of them are old and structural. OctoMap clamps each cell's log-odds between fixed bounds, so that a cell observed occupied a thousand times can still be cleared by a few contradicting rays; clamping keeps the map able to change, but it acts only on cells that are observed again [@hornung2013octomap].
